Zoroaster is known throughout the entire Orient as the lawgiver and founder of the teachings of the **Magi** <term>Magi: ancient Persian priests and sages from whom the word "magic" originates</term>; the Greeks also became acquainted with him, particularly during Alexander’s campaign and the conquest of Persia, under the name Zarates <note>original: "Zarates"</note>. Their accounts, as far as history is concerned, also agree reasonably well with the monuments preserved in the ancient writings of the **Parsees** <term>Parsees: the Zoroastrian community that preserved the ancient Persian religious traditions</term>. However, Zoroaster himself only claims to be the restorer of this law, and names **Hom** <note>likely referring to Haoma, both a sacred plant and a divinity in Zoroastrian tradition</note> as the one [who...]

<margin>
a) The name Zoroaster also originates from the Greeks; in the current Parsee language he is called Zerdust. In the original Zend language <note>Zend: the language of the Avesta, the sacred scriptures of Zoroastrianism</note>, his name was *Zeretoschtro*, which was called *Zertoscht* in the subsequent Pahlavi language. Those who search for the meaning of names find—and have found after much laborious investigation—that *Zeretoschtro* was a surname for Cham <note>The author likely refers to Ham, the son of Noah, reflecting an older scholarly tradition of linking biblical figures to Persian history</note>, which means **Gold Star**. In the ancient Zend language, *Zere* means Gold, and *Toschter* is a guardian of the stars, one of their worshipped protective spirits who bestows rain upon the world.
</margin>

### Zoroaster

who first planted the true knowledge of God among this people. About this **Hom** <note>likely referring to Haoma, here personified as an ancient sage or divinity; the text notes he is the source of the teachings Zoroaster later codified</note> there is much uncertain talk; at times his life is placed so far back that he is said to be the fifth in descending line from Noah. More commonly, his life is set during the reign of **Djemschid** <term>Djemschid: also known as Jamshid, a legendary king of the Golden Age in Persian mythology who is said to have brought civilization to mankind</term>, who is identified in these books as the true founder of the Persian Empire (approximately a thousand years before Zoroaster). Hom or **Haomo** was the first lawgiver of this people, whom the **Parsees** still revere as their protective spirit; Djemschid accepted his law and introduced it among his people, ensuring it was put into practice. He and his people were worshippers of the Creator of nature and His work. The Parsees say of him that, without knowing specific religious ceremonies, he was content with practicing the essentials of faith. This era is called the age of the **Poeriodekeschaus** <term>Paoiryo-tkaesha: "those of the first law," referring to the earliest believers and righteous ancestors who lived before Zoroaster’s formal revelation</term> (Men of the First Law), and the description they give of it resembles the patriarchal state found in the writings of Moses. Under **Gustasp** <note>King Vishtaspa, the royal patron who protected Zoroaster and helped spread his teachings</note> (around 550 years before the Christian era), the law of the worshippers of **Ormuzd** <term>Ormuzd: Ahura Mazda, the "Wise Lord" and supreme deity of Zoroastrianism</term> and the religious service were established by Zoroaster who, as he says of himself, collected, expanded, and formed the teachings of Hom into a cohesive whole.

Regarding the homeland of Zoroaster, Anquetil <note>Abraham Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron (1731–1805), the French orientalist who brought the first Zend-Avesta manuscripts to Europe</note> has provided very convincing evidence for Iran, specifically the region between the rivers **Araxes** and **Cyrus** <note>modern-day Aras and Kura rivers in the Caucasus region</note>, and even more precisely **Aderbedjan** <note>Azerbaijan</note>, which is a part of northern Me-

->as a religious teacher.<-

...identified his role as a religious teacher, and his birthplace was **Urmia** (also called Urmi, Ariema, or Arimat). <note>Urmia is a city in northwestern Iran; in Zoroastrian tradition, it is often associated with the prophet's birthplace.</note> Whenever these **Zend-books** <term>Zend-books: the Zend-Avesta, the primary collection of sacred Zoroastrian scriptures</term> speak of this land, it is preferentially called the "pure Iran" and is cited as the favorite land of **Ormuzd** <term>Ormuzd: Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity and "Wise Lord" of Zoroastrianism</term>, upon which he has placed his most exceptional blessing; likewise, **Ariema** <note>likely a reference to Airyanem Vaejah, the mythical homeland of the early Iranians</note> is called the source of all blessing (on account of the Law).

These books also describe the location of the land by the mountains and waters that surround it, of which they speak with much exaggeration. Among the mountains, **Albordj** <term>Albordj: the Alborz or Elburz mountain range in northern Iran</term>, at whose foot this land lies, is especially praised; indeed, in the Zend-books, it is even cited as the foundation and the root of the entire earth, where **Djemschid** <term>Djemschid: Jamshid, a legendary king of the Persian Golden Age</term> also had his fortress and royal seat. Albordj—the great and sublime Albordj—is the **Caucasus** mountain range, which rises on the northern and western sides of the Caspian Sea.

In the **Bun-Dehesch** <term>Bun-Dehesch: the Bundahishn, an encyclopedic collection of Zoroastrian cosmogony and mythology</term>, it is said that within two hundred years, all the mountains on earth—numbering 244—grew up from Albordj. Among these is the excellent and great **Tireh Albordj**, the "back" of the **Tschekant Danti** <term>Tschekant Danti: Chakat-i-Daitik, the "Peak of the Law," a mythical mountain where the judgment of the soul takes place</term> and **Arzur**. This Tschekant Danti, [near] the Caspian Sea, is spoken of just as frequently. Its depth is depicted, and beneath it lies the **Tschinevad Bridge** <term>Tschinevad: the Chinvat Bridge or "Bridge of the Separator," which souls must cross after death to be judged</term>, across which departed souls must pass to reach the "Abode of Joy." In the Bun-Dehesch, it is stated: "The Tschekant Danti is in the middle of the world; it is a hundred men deep, and beneath it is the Tschinevad Bridge; there the souls must give an account <note>original: "Rechen-schaft"</note> of their deeds."

The **Parsis** <term>Parsis: the Zoroastrian community in India</term> trace **Zoroaster’s** descent from the ancient royal family, from the lineage of **Minotscher** <term>Minotscher: Manuchehr, a legendary king of the Pishdadian dynasty</term>, who was a descendant of **Feridun** <term>Feridun: Fereydun, a celebrated heroic king of ancient Persia</term>. Feridun was one of their most beloved kings and is said to have held the seat of his empire in **Azerbaijan** (where **Urmi** <note>Urmia, a city in northwestern Iran</note> is located). The existing stories of his birth and his life are of too recent an origin (b) for one to be able to guarantee everything. Yet this circumstance may excuse the many fabulous elements with which his birth and childhood years, in particular, have been embellished; or one might rather wish to find here a new proof that the birth of extraordinary men has always been linked with extraordinary circumstances. At the very least, these stories testify to the respect and high opinion that his followers hold for their Prophet,

Whoever walks **Ahriman’s** impure path, from his body shall flow streams of blood, and he will be handed over to the flames of fire. Know the meaning of this fire: a generation of men will abandon the Law and run after **Ahriman**. The sickness of doubt will torment them, but my **Mobedis** <term>Mobedis: Zoroastrian priests who serve as guardians of the faith and the sacred fire</term> shall fight against them, and this stream of fire shall consume them." Now **Ormuzd** taught him the **Zend-Avesta** <note>The primary collection of religious texts in Zoroastrianism</note>.

# Zoroaster

...listened to him, until he publicly declared himself a messenger of God. "I have come forth from God," he addressed the King <note>King Gustasp, the first royal patron of Zoroastrianism</note>, "who made the seven heavens, the earth, and the stars; from the God who gives life and nourishment to all, and who looks after His servant—He who placed the crown upon you and protects you, and who drew your body out of nothingness. Through Him you rule, and have power over your servants." 

He handed him the **Avesta** <note>The primary collection of sacred texts in Zoroastrianism</note> and spoke further: "God has sent me to the nations so that they may accept this word in **Zend** <note>The language in which the Avesta was written, or its traditional interpretation</note> as **Ormuzd’s** <note>The supreme creator deity, Ahura Mazda</note> will. If you do God's will, you shall have glory in the next world as in this one; but if you do not hear His word, God in His wrath will break your crown, and your end shall be **Duzakh** <note>Hell, or the place of punishment/abyss</note>. Incline your ear to the teachings of **Ormuzd** and no longer do the will of the **Dews** <note>The **Daevas**, ancient Persian demons or malevolent spirits representing chaos and disorder</note>." 

The King demanded signs and miracles from him. "Read the **Zend-Avesta**," said the Prophet, "then you will need no miracles: the book itself, which you see here, is miracle enough. It will teach you what exists in both worlds, the course of the stars, and the path of the good." 

When, after some time, through the intrigues of the courtiers who were envious of him, **Zoroaster** was decried as a deceiver and even as a sorcerer, he resolved to perform a miracle by healing the King's horse, which no physician and no wise man could do. The King then considered him a prophet and accepted the **Avesta**, which he read diligently and had explained to him by **Zoroaster**.

"I now demand four things from you," said the King, once he had already fully surrendered himself to *Zoroaster*, "which are just as great and wonderful as the law of God: 1) to know what place is destined for me in the next world; 2) to be invulnerable to enemies; 3) that I be equipped with knowledge of everything that happens in the world; and 4) that my soul remain in the body until the resurrection."

# Holy Books

...also of the immortality of the soul. These seem to have been ancient, traditional beliefs among the Persians which, although obscured and distorted, could never be entirely eradicated; and whenever they appeared in a suitable guise, they were welcomed back with applause. In Zoroaster's system, these elements formed the fundamental teachings; and just as he himself refers here to antiquity—the times of a **Hom** <note>original: "Hom". Refers to Haoma, an ancient divinity and a sacred plant/drink in Indo-Iranian tradition, often personified as a primordial priest or prophet who preceded Zoroaster.</note>—and presents himself merely as a restorer of these teachings, I do not hesitate to accept these principles as old, well-known doctrines among this people.

His teaching on the origin of evil through **Ahriman** <term>Ahriman: The Middle Persian name for Angra Mainyu, the "Destructive Spirit" and personification of evil, who exists in eternal opposition to the creator god</term> was a very fine and artful tapestry; and considering how much the wise have always tormented themselves with this doctrine <note>The "problem of evil" or theodicy—the question of how evil can exist in a world created by a good deity—is a central challenge in many religions.</note>, he maintained a sensible middle path. His Ahriman, on one hand, had also sprung from **unbounded time** <note>This refers to *Zrvan Akarana*, or "Infinite Time," which in some Zoroastrian traditions was seen as the primordial origin from which both the good god and the evil spirit emerged.</note>; he was a self-creator and powerful enough to defy **Ormuzd** <term>Ormuzd: The Middle Persian name for Ahura Mazda, the supreme "Wise Lord" and god of light, wisdom, and goodness</term> in his world of light—who, according to the decree of eternal time, even had to grant him certain periods of dominance, thus being powerful and strong enough to do and cause evil. On the other hand, light and purity frightened him and could render him powerless—and he himself will ultimately become light again. <note>This refers to the Zoroastrian concept of *Frashokereti*, the final renovation of the universe where evil is destroyed or transformed, and all creation is purified.</note>

This system alone testifies to Zoroaster's broad-minded spirit and his sound judgment in extricating himself from the snares in which human reason has always become entangled; just as his doctrine of the **Feruers** <term>Feruers: Also known as Fravashis, these are the pre-existing souls or guardian spirits of all beings, representing the divine spark within humans and the cosmos</term> from a to the deepest...

->## of the Parsis<-

...testifies to a bright and speculative <note>In this context, "speculative" refers to deep philosophical or theoretical thinking rather than financial risk.</note> mind, which brings honor to humanity in every age and among every people. And these were undoubtedly **Zoroaster’s** own teachings. Of all the others that appear in this system, I do not venture to assert this with such certainty. Even among the **Parsi writings** <term>Parsi writings: The sacred texts of the Zoroastrian community, who are known as Parsis (meaning "Persians") in India.</term> themselves, if one reads them with diligence, one finds a great difference regarding their content and teachings. This investigation would lead me too far from my purpose here, yet I consider it my duty to alert my readers to this. Perhaps in the course of time you will discover for yourselves the progress of the doctrines—which is admittedly only slight—or at least you will then find what was taught in the time of Zoroaster, and what teachings subsequent ages produced.

# Sacred Books

A dialect known as **Pazend** <term>Pazend: A supplementary system used to explain or transliterate the Avestan "Zend" texts, often used to make the ancient scriptures more accessible to priests while remaining mysterious to the public.</term> also descends from Zend; according to the nature of the language, it literally means "corrupted Zend." The question: What within the <term>Parsi|A community in India and elsewhere that follows the Zoroastrian faith, descended from Persian refugees who fled Islamic persecution in the 7th–10th centuries.</term> religious system was the ancient, genuine teaching of Zoroaster, and what should be regarded as additions from his followers and successors? can probably no longer be determined with full certainty; and upon careful examination, the conclusion is that the oldest teachings have been made completely unrecognizable through the fabric woven by his followers, so that while one can now provide an account and report of the Parsi religion for approximately the last thousand years, the earlier times fall into a darkness. One cannot help oneself in this regard except by extracting simple, basic dogmas—which one encounters in the <term>Vendidad|A collection of texts within the Avesta primarily concerned with ecclesiastical laws and ritual purification.</term> and the <term>Izeshnes|Also known as the Yasna, these are the primary liturgical texts of the Zoroastrian tradition.</term> often only as hints—and accepting them as the foundation upon which later eras built their edifice and organized it into a system. If one excludes these songs and the Vendidad, which constitutes a small part of the Avesta and has been preserved from the ruins, the sources are far too recent to recognize Zoroaster’s specific teachings. Creation from nothingness was an absurd thought to him; and what he found in visible nature, he applied to the spirit world, and from there to God. For the physical world, he conceived of a seed to which he gave the form of a bull <note>This refers to Gavaevodata, the primordial "Uniquely Created Bull" in Zoroastrian mythology, from whose marrow and spirit all life was said to spring.</note>, in which God had placed all the germs for the subsequent humans, animals, plants, <term>etc.|original: "zc.", an archaic abbreviation for "et cetera".</term> which He later formed; and since this was not yet sufficient for the ensouled creatures (this was only the outer shell, and according to his system, it seems he considered all of nature to be ensouled), the idea, the conception, the image that the Creator thought of all His creatures had to provide the first foundation for all existing beings; thoughts and ideas in God which He realized—not merely as a norm and plan for creation and the creatures, but as self-existing beings that animated the physical world. <note>The author is describing the *Fravashis*, which in Zoroastrianism are the pre-existing spiritual essences or "prototypes" of all beings.</note> And according to this thought, the doctrine of God the Creator was also measured. He pushed this ground, this source, back into eternity: and so this eternity, a limitless time, a time without time, became the primal source from which God Himself had sprung. In a certain sense, a beginningless, nameless, and unthinkable being was established as God; nevertheless, according to this system, God had emerged, and as it is explicitly stated in the *Ulema-i Islam* <term>Ulema-i Islam|A Zoroastrian theological text from the medieval period, written in New Persian, which discusses the primacy of Time.</term> <note>original: "Eulma Eslam"</note>, He was begotten of limitless time <note>This refers to *Zurvan Akarana* (Infinite Time), the central concept of "Zervanism," a branch of Zoroastrianism that posited Time as the father of both the good God (Ahura Mazda) and the evil spirit (Ahriman).</note> before time even was.

This boundless and nameless eternity was at once the source of the primal light, primal fire, and primal water; or, the seed of that which later, at the beginning of all beings, became light, fire, and water, lay hidden within this boundless time. <note>The author is referring to the Zoroastrian concept of *Zurvan Akarana*, or "Infinite Time," which pre-exists even the creator god.</note>

# Ormuzd

begotten as the firstborn of the Eternal and Unfathomable. <note>Ormuzd is the Middle Persian name for Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity of Zoroastrianism.</note> The imprint of the eternal Godhead, the radiant image of infinite life-force, in whom all infinity, glory, and attributes of the Eternal are to be found, dwelling in the primal light, the throne of eternity. Therefore, he is the highest wisdom, and his power and active spirit (will) are boundlessly holy down to the very root of his being. The highest judge of the world, king of all beings in purest justice, goodness, light, and radiance. His dwelling and covering is purest light.

This calculation and determination of the twelve thousand years in the Parsi system <term>Parsi system: the religious traditions and interpretations of the Zoroastrians</term> had its origin in astronomy—in the sun's path through the twelve signs of the zodiac in the heavens. In the ***Bundahishn*** <term>Bundahishn: "Primal Creation," a foundational Zoroastrian text that describes cosmogony and the nature of the spirit world</term>, these celestial bodies—or rather their **Izeds** <term>Izeds: Yazatas, or divine beings "worthy of worship" who serve as guardians of the natural and spiritual realms</term> and their dominion—are discussed, to each of whom a duration of a thousand years is assigned; these conclude with the cycle of twelve thousand years. Everything visible was a symbol of the invisible; this was especially true of the heavenly hosts—the sun, the moon, and the stars—which were all an image of the spirit world. In them and through them, the **Izeds** reigned. It is well known that the twelve heavenly signs were sacred to the **Chaldeans** <term>Chaldeans: inhabitants of Babylonia famous in antiquity for their mastery of astronomy and astrology</term> and the **Magi** <term>Magi: the priestly class of ancient Persia, from whose name the word "magic" is derived</term>, and here this circle becomes a representation of the cycle of the world age. Thus the sun, like a courageous hero, traverses the twelve signs of heaven in one year through alternating phases, and twelve thousand are the years of the eternal. With their conclusion, Ormuzd's reign ends. This time is divided into four periods. ## Of the Creatures of Ormuzd.

---

Ormuzd, in light and goodness, conceived the spiritual and physical world, and every thought became a being, became the spirit of a potent essence, the purest image of future existing things that were to dwell in Ormuzd's world: entirely light and spirit, in essence spirit and in life spirit—thus arose
->the **Feruers**,<-
the first creatures of Ormuzd. Thoughts, ideas in God, which were realized <note>These "Feruers" correspond to the *Fravashis* in modern scholarship—the eternal, spiritual blueprints or guardian spirits of all living things</note>.

<header>System of Doctrine of the Parsis.</header>

This is the system of the **Parsis** <term>Parsis: Members of the Zoroastrian community, followers of the prophet Zoroaster</term> regarding God and
the origin of all things, with which all their other
teachings stand in connection and harmony; yet 
it is not only the teachings—their entire religious practice 
relates to it. According to this system, 
the religion and the content of the law of the Parsis 
is a war against **Ahriman** and his realm. The 
**Parsi** considers himself called as a warrior who 
is meant to strike the **Dews** <note>Dews: Also known as Daevas; these are the demonic spirits of the Zoroastrian tradition</note> and thereby enlarge 
and increase **Ormuzd’s** <note>Ormuzd: Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity of light and wisdom</note> realm. **Ahriman** is indeed 
a powerful spirit to him, but he can be 
conquered and rendered powerless through light and 
purity. And thus, the entire religious practice of 
the Parsis becomes—**purifications**. Not only is this 
the content of most prayers, through which they 
draw close to the **Izeds** <note>Izeds: The Yazatas, divine beings or "angels" who assist Ormuzd in the cosmic struggle</note> in order to 
collectively wage war against **Ahriman**, but it is also 
the concept behind the moral precepts: to wage war against 
and incapacitate **Ahriman** through the purity 
of thoughts, words, and the heart. It is furthermore 
the substance of all liturgical ordinances and 
purifications by which the **Dews**—who poison 
and defile humans, trees, animals, earth, and water—are 
driven away and defeated. **Ahriman** hates them 
and seeks to make them unhappy; he pursues 
them even in death. Therefore, such 
precautions must also be applied to 
corpses so that they may have peace and security 
from the **Dews**. The departed soul is exposed 
to a similar persecution, which, although as a worshiper 
of **Ormuzd**—

[...what they] are, is not easy to determine. The fundamental idea that prevails in this system—that "from nothing, nothing comes" <note>original: "Aus Nichts wird Nichts," echoing the ancient principle *ex nihilo nihil fit*</note> and that for everything that exists, a germ or seed must have previously existed—undoubtedly belongs to **Zoroaster**. This concept even extends to the origin of **Ormuzd** <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity of light and wisdom</note>, who had his germ, his foundation, in **unlimited time** <note>Zervan Akarana: The concept of infinite time as the source of both good and evil deities</note>; and of this time, nothing can be said, for it became almost an abstract idea. Before **Ormuzd** could create beings outside of himself, his thoughts—his mental image of these future things—had to become the seed, since **Zoroaster** personified them; these were the **Fravashis** <note>original: "Feruers". In Zoroastrianism, these are the pre-existing spiritual essences or guardian spirits of all beings</note>. These, as now self-existing beings, received power and life, and the spiritual qualities necessary to animate and enliven. Yet this was not yet sufficient for the corporeal world, which was matter. The **Bundahishn** <term>Bun-Dehesch: An important collection of Zoroastrian cosmogony and cosmology, written in Middle Persian</term> describes a mechanism <note>original: "Maschine", used here to mean a primal biological structure or vessel</note> arising which enclosed within itself the seed and germ of future things that were subsequently developed: the **Bull** <note>Gavaevodata: The primordial bull from whose body all life and plants eventually sprang</note>. It describes water arising through the influence of the stars, as well as a mountain that gradually grows to a tremendous height and, through its roots, became the foundation and the linking-together of the earth; nevertheless, we have not yet fully unlocked and developed **Zoroaster's** idea in this.

**Ahriman** <note>Angra Mainyu: The destructive spirit and adversary of Ormuzd</note> was also equipped with creative power because of his origin, just like **Ormuzd**. To distinguish between these two different kinds of creation, every creature received something of the seed of the one from whom it had originated:

It is obvious that all these teachings have, over such a vast span of time, taken on a more regular form but have also received many additions; this is all the less surprising, as it is a natural consequence of the spirit of inquiry, and because the records of **Zoroaster** <note>Zarathustra: the ancient Persian prophet</note>—which could have settled these matters most decisively—had been lost except for a few remnants, leaving much room for those eager for knowledge to indulge in their own inventions. Nevertheless, despite all this, it remains true: an overview of this system as a whole, especially the fundamental doctrines upon which the entire structure rests and which undoubtedly stem from antiquity, reveals—even if one wipes away the modern **embellishments** <note>original: "Schmink" (literally "makeup" or "paint"), suggesting later superficial additions to the core truth</note>—the great, all-encompassing spirit of the founder. He was able to break through so many difficulties and mists that had so greatly obscured and distorted the doctrine of the **One God** as **Creator of the world**, and to seek out once more the old path, which was purer. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Zoroaster as a reformer rather than an inventor of a new religion, linking his teachings back to the mythical King Jamshid. It transitions from the historical context to the specific theological nature of Ormuzd (Ahura Mazda).</meta>

->### System of Doctrine<-

[years] ago known to **Djemschid** <note>Jamshid: a mythical Great King of ancient Iran who reigned during a golden age before the rise of Zoroastrianism</note>, and accepted and practiced by him; that he [Zoroaster] was actually only the restorer of these ancient teachings and the reformer. What could be expected from a sharp-thinking mind in this regard was achieved by **Zoroaster**, as he himself placed speculative teachings in such a light that they were bound to be fruitful in their consequences. Look at his doctrine of **Ormuzd** <note>Ahura Mazda: the creator god and highest deity of Zoroastrianism, representing light and order</note> and **Ahriman** <note>Angra Mainyu: the destructive spirit or personification of evil and darkness</note>, which he placed alongside one another so that they could become the most fertile source for the cultivation of man.

**Ormuzd**, begotten from light-seeds by the Eternal and dwelling in the light. He [the Eternal] did indeed give him a beginning, but deep within eternity, and he [Ormuzd] became a partaker of all the sublime qualities of the Unfathomable. Never yet has a human understanding, through its own reflection, better raised itself out of these depths. **Ormuzd’s** light became life, life-force, goodness—the **Primal Word** <note>original: "Urwort"; refers to the creative or divine logos</note>. From him, light and life, spiritual power, and truth flow to everyone. His worshipers, brought to life through his word, draw near to him and his light, and thereby have fellowship with him and the blessed spirits surrounding him (the **Amschaspands** <note>Amesha Spentas: "Bounteous Immortals," a class of six or seven divine beings who represent aspects of the creation</note> and **Izeds** <note>Yazatas: "beings worthy of worship," divine spirits or angels below the Amschaspands</note>). For **Ormuzd** shares his light with the world and enlivens all things: the tree as well as the noble human, the animal as well as the **Amschaspand**. What direction of the heart might such teachings not produce? In their application, they also became the basis for the conception and the requirement in the law of pu- <note>The word is completed by the catchword: purity (Reinigkeit)</note>

# [of] the Parsis. <note>original: "der Parsen"; refers to the followers of Zoroastrianism</note>

...purity of mankind, purity in thoughts, in words, and in actions—such were the consequences Zoroaster drew from this teaching.

Because **Ahriman** was presented in darkness as the sole author of all evil and all vices, and because his efforts and those of all the **Dews** <term>Dews: Daevas; in Zoroastrianism, these are malevolent spirits or demons that choose to serve the principle of evil</term> were depicted as harmful and hostile to humanity—and because, in this regard, every **Mazdeiesnan** <term>Mazdeiesnan: a "Mazda-worshiper" or follower of the religion of Ormuzd (Ahura Mazda)</term> was instructed to view himself as a born warrior against all darkness—imagine what impressions this made against evil, and against all defilements of the body and the soul! Even physical impurities were regarded as hiding places in which **Dews** concealed themselves to gain power over human beings. From this idea sprang the many legal prescriptions concerning purifications and the mandatory rules of caution intended to avoid all types of defilement. This practice was already considered a victory over the **Dews**, bringing purity and light into **Ormuzd’s** realm.

However, it is just as clearly evident that these teachings lacked the proper support to make them more beneficial to the common good, and that their entire strength was stripped away by a misguided direction. The greater part of the legal prescriptions and requirements bore the mark of that era; they were not instructions for the cultivation of the heart, but rather sensory ceremonies that occupied the **Mazdeiesnans**. These rituals were presented as being so important that it was as if the light and purity of the heart...

## System of Doctrine
E 2
<meta>catchword: These</meta>

...[of the] heart were effected. <note>The text completes the word "Herzens" (heart) from the previous page.</note> And yet, the Parsis <note>original: "Parsen"; followers of Zoroastrianism in India</note> were just as much human beings as the Europeans. — Even Anquetil, the great admirer of this system, admits that a punctuality in these prescribed ceremonies, an anxiety not to overlook anything or to neglect the prescribed times, or to omit even a single word in the prayers, constitutes the primary work of the religious Parsis: That the sanctity of their worship has shifted almost entirely into the sanctity of the languages in which it is conducted—languages that even the <term>Mobeds</term> (priests) do not understand; and when they have recited these strange, unknown words, they say: they have performed divine service. Such a turn in religion, where merely external legalistic acts, performed mechanically, constitute the worship—and even the legislator provided the guidance for this—what is to be expected from it? Even in the <term>Avesta</term> <note>the primary collection of Zoroastrian religious texts</note>, the merit of the external in religion is ranked higher than the good deeds of men. Of the latter, it is often said: it shall be credited to him as if he had read a thousand <term>Izeshnes</term> <note>Yasna; the primary liturgical collection of texts and the ritual of the same name</note>, and the recitation of the <term>Izeshnes</term> saves one from <term>Duzakh</term> <note>Zoroastrian concept of Hell</note> w).

of the Parsis.

E 3

These prescribed prayer formulas are, according to the Avesta, the most important of the Parsi duties: prayers for all activities and affairs of this life; for every time of day and night, for extraordinary occurrences of life; and their punctual recitation is the hallmark of true <term>Mazdayasnians</term> <note>original: "Mazdeisnans"; those who worship Ahura Mazda</note>. They must occasionally endure with patience the five-to-sixfold repetition of the same prayer in succession, and often the omission of a single word can make the entire action vain. Nevertheless, in various instances, they can also commission a priest for a specific price to perform this task, who then attends to this exercise in their name. Alongside these prayers, the prescribed purification ceremonies constitute the greatest part of their duties. Purifications, which accumulate here even more than among the Jews in the Old Testament, since according to this system multiple defilements are possible through the <term>Daevas</term> <note>original: "Dews"; malevolent spirits or demons</note>, who cling to every unclean place and must be driven out again. As a struggle and victory against <term>Ahriman</term> <note>the personification of evil and darkness</note> and his kingdom, these become an unceasing duty and the primary business of the Parsi.

# Divine Service
<meta>catchword: face</meta>

their head is the **Desturan Destur** (**Chief Magus** <note>original Latin: "Archimagus"</note>). The priest in sacred service, for as long as he performs that service, is the **Djuti** <note>the chief officiating priest</note>; his servants and assistants in the sacred work, who are also priests, are called **Raspi** <note>assistant priests who tend the fire</note>. Divine service must be held in a consecrated place (at the fire-temple <note>original: "Feuerkapelle" (fire chapel)</note>) and consists of the reading of liturgical prayers, depending on the nature of the place or the occasion of the **Vendidad** <note>a collection of texts within the Avesta focused on religious law and ritual purity</note>. For this, a sacred vessel with fire is required at all times, in the presence of which the liturgy is read (the common **Parsi** performs his prayers only before the kitchen fire). The **Barsom** x) is also required, and the **Djuti** must be covered with the **Penom** y).

---

x) The **Barsom** is a bundle or cluster of pomegranate, tamarisk, or date branches, which are tied together by a crafted band (**Evanguin**) made from a green twig. The number of branches depends on the solemnity of the service (either 23, 35, or 75); it must be held by the priest in his left hand during the reading. In India, brass wire is used for the **Barsom** instead of branches. Some festivals also require that the officiating priest (**Djuti**), during the reading, must eat bread (**Darun bread**) and meat (**Myazd** <note>original: "Miedz"</note>) which the **Parsi** brings as an offering, and drink the **Haoma juice** (**Parahaoma** <note>original: "Homsaft" / "Perahom"</note>). This gives great power to the service and brings blessings upon the **Parsis**.

y) The **Penom** <note>now commonly known as a Padan; a ritual mouth-mask</note> is a kind of pouch or a cloth, approximately 6 inches square, which covers the lower part of the fa- <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "sichts" from the OCR indicates the full word is "Gesichts" (face).</note>

The prescribed prayers (**Izeschne's** <note>Yasnas; the primary liturgical acts and hymns of the Avesta</note>) at the designated times are especially those directed to the various **Gahs** (**divisions of the day**, for every time of day and night has its own **Ized** <note>Yazata; a "worthy of worship" divine being or angel</note> as a protector). The seven summer months are divided into five **Gahs**, and the five winter months into four. The first is **Gah Havan** <note>Hawan Gah</note> at sunrise; the second is **Gah Rapitan** <note>Rapithwin Gah</note> at noon; the third is **Gah Osiren** <note>Uzayarin Gah</note> at 3 o'clock in the afternoon; the fourth is **Gah Evesuthrem** <note>Aiwisruthrem Gah</note> when the stars begin to become visible; and the fifth is **Gah Oschem** <note>Ushahin Gah</note> at midnight. In the winter months, **Gah Rapitan** is omitted. For **Ized Rapitan**, as the overseer of warmth, goes beneath the earth in winter to warm it and to revive nature once again. In addition to these, a **Jescht** <note>Yasht; a hymn of praise</note> must be offered to the specific **Ized** of each day. For all days of every month are distributed among the **Izeds**, to which the **Amschaspands** <note>Amesha Spentas; the six "Bounteous Immortals" or archangels</note> also belong, where they rule specifically and bless mankind.

When the **Vendidad** <note>the "Law against the Daevas," a text focused on ritual purity</note> is read, it must necessarily be joined <note>original German: "vergesellschaftet" (associated/joined)</note> with the **Vispered** <note>a liturgical extension of the Yasna</note> and the **Izeschne**—

Apart from this liturgical reading and praying, there are also prescriptions for the common Parsi, composed as prayers which he recites in his everyday language. These are of various kinds. Some, which he pronounces upon rising, washing his hands, or putting on the *Kosti* z), are called *Nerengs* <note>Nirangs; short ritual formulas or incantations</note>.

The *Patets* are prayers of repentance, and their *Afergans* and *Afrins* are thanksgivings and blessings.

### Holy Fire of the Parsis.
E 5
<meta>catchword: who</meta>

is represented. Light and the brilliance of fire are symbols of his deity, and according to Parsi doctrine, fire is an emanation of the spirit and power of God, the purest symbol of the incessantly active, life-giving deity. They believe in a primordial fire, of which material fire is the image. The former is the bond of union between Ormuzd <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity of Zoroastrianism</note> and the essence entwined in eternity; it is at the same time the seed from which Ormuzd begat all beings: and what Ormuzd begets from his seed is called his son. Therefore, Amesha Spentas <note>Amschaspands; the "Bounteous Immortals" or archangels</note>, Yazatas <note>Izeds; "beings worthy of worship" or angels</note>, stars, humans, animals, and plants are all called sons of God, because all these creatures have something of the divine living seed within them. Ormuzd's fire is, in their conception, the most holy and sublime. The symbol of this is the Behram fire <note>Atash Behram, the "Fire of Victory," the highest grade of ritual fire</note> (earthly holy fire in the temple); therefore, this is also the most sacred to them: Just as every fire in their houses is also holy to them, which is carefully preserved from all impurity so that nothing defiling can fall into it, before which the Parsi performs his usual prayer, and by which the Mobed <note>a high-ranking Zoroastrian priest</note> is also permitted in special cases of necessity to read his *Izeschne* <note>Yasna; the primary liturgical act and its accompanying texts</note> (in the Zend language <note>Avestan</note>).

---

The Behram fire, which is used in the temple on the *Atash-dan* <note>Atesch-dan; a fire altar or urn, approximately 3 feet in diameter at the top in the shape of an open rose, upon which the fire burns</note>

# 74

->Holy Fire<-

to be [consecrated], it must be purified nine times <note>original: "neunmahl geläutert seyn"; This refers to the ritual process of "recycling" fire to increase its purity</note> *), and the sacred fire is called **Aderan** <term>Atash Adaran; the "Fire of Fires," the second highest grade of consecrated fire in Zoroastrianism</term>. This fire, which must be constantly served by two to three **Mobeds** <term>Zoroastrian priests</term>, receives offerings of pure incense thrown upon it, as well as pure wood that is donated and brought for that purpose. Such offerings can and must also be brought to the other fires.

Every city must have a **Dad-gah** <term>Atash Dadgah; the third grade of sacred fire, which can be housed in a temple or a home</term> (fire temple), and every village and inhabited place must have an **Aderan-shah** (a place where the holy fire is maintained), both for divine service and to protect every fire from all impurity. According to this system of the **Parsis**, every kitchen fire, once it has been used three times, is brought to the **Aderan**. Furthermore, there are various specific holy days among them when all fires from the houses must be brought to the **Aderan**; the **Aderan** itself is carried annually (according to some, every three years) to the **Behram fire** <note>Atash Behram; the "Fire of Victory," the highest and most sacred grade of Zoroastrian fire</note>. Strictly speaking, every province or large city should have a **Behram fire**. After the passage of a certain time

---

a) It is drawn from the common fire, such that one makes a distinct new fire from it using pure wood; from this, a fire is drawn a second time and maintained in a third place. From this, it is drawn again to a fourth place, and in this manner until the ninth time; then it is the holiest and purest.

# Holy Water of the Parsis.

...are just as lofty and varied as those regarding fire. It belongs to the primordial seed of all beings: the purest celestial water stands before the throne of Ormuzd <term>Ahura Mazda, the supreme creator deity</term>, and is the holy and beloved daughter of Ormuzd; it brings all of nature to life, cleanses the body, and provides it with life-giving nourishment. Furthermore, Ormuzd gave it to mankind as a defensive shield against the Dews <term>Daevas, or malevolent spirits</term>, in order to render their influences powerless and harmless. It possesses a holy and powerful Ized <term>Yazata, a divinity or angelic being in Zoroastrianism</term> who must be invoked at the first crowing of the cock. Water, just like fire, is a symbol of everything good and pure. Just as fire permeates all creatures and brings forth the effects of life within them, so too does water, which contains within itself the vital essence of all humans, animals, and plants. It is therefore sacred and is the means by which human beings are sanctified and purified.

The Parsis have two particularly holy waters: *Zur* <note>also known as Zor, consecrated water used in the Yasna ceremony</note> and *Hom*. *Zur* is ordinary water that must be prepared under special ceremonies and prayers at the midnight hour, and it serves in divine worship. *Hom* is the juice of the Hom-tree <note>the Haoma plant, known for its ritual importance and intoxicating or healing properties</note>, the tree of immortality, and it is the "water of life."

The *Zur*-water is prepared at night from any water that has been made *padiav* <term>Padyab, a term for ritual washing or making something ritually clean</term>, that is, made pure. A source of water is made *padiav* when the priest pours it three times from one vessel into another, during which he recites the prayers with a loud voice.

# Purifications of the Parsis

...my wishes publicly until the resurrection, where I shall proclaim his praise. "Abundance and **Paradise**" <note>original: "Ueberfluß und *Behescht*"; *Behesht* refers to the Zoroastrian concept of heaven or paradise. This phrase likely refers to the *Ashem Vohu* prayer</note> etc.

2) **Ghosel** <note>original: "*Ghosel*"; refers to the *Ghusl*, a ritual purification of the entire body</note>. This is a simple washing of the whole body with bull’s urine (<term>Nereng gomez din</term> <note>original: "*Nereng gomez din*"; refers to consecrated bull's urine used in rituals</note> is what it is called when it has been sanctified by the priests), after which one dries oneself with earth and then washes again with water, and prays the **Badj Serosch** <note>original: "*Badj Serosch*"; the *Baj* or prayer dedicated to the angel Sraosha</note> with the following words:

I lift up my praise to **Serosch**, bless him with strength; he is pure, strong, and shining in **Ormuzd’s** <note>original: "*Ormuzd*"; Ahura Mazda, the supreme God</note> glory. Grow ever more in radiance and bliss. "Abundance and Paradise" etc. "That is **Ormuzd’s** will" <note>referring to the *Ahuna Vairya* prayer</note> etc. five times.

3) **Baraschnom** <note>original: "*Baraschnom*"; the *Bareshnum-nu-shab*, the most rigorous Zoroastrian purification ritual lasting nine nights</note>, the purification of nine nights, is the most powerful of all purifications. The area is strewn with sand, and no one except a holy man well-versed in the law, who belongs to the family of a **Destur** <note>original: "*Destur*"; a high priest</note>, may administer the **Baraschnom**. ### of the Parsis.

->F 5<-

These various kinds of purifications are determined in their application partly by the different possible impurities, which have their own various degrees and stages, and partly by the holiness and importance of the task the Parsi is performing.

Without first performing <term>padiav</term> <note>original: *padiav*; a minor ritual washing of the face, hands, and feet while reciting prayers</note> upon himself or the vessel he intends to use, he undertakes almost no action of ordinary life, for fear that this or that might be impure. What other nations might recommend as mere physical cleanliness is, to him, already sacred as a matter of religion.

Beyond these natural impurities, according to the Parsi system, a higher degree of contamination is caused by <term>Kharfesters</term> <note>original: *Kharfesters*; noxious or harmful creatures such as insects, reptiles, or amphibians, believed to be created by the evil spirit Ahriman</note> (such as toads or snakes, etc.) that touch something, whereby it becomes in their language <term>her</term> (impure). This is especially true of <term>hernessa</term>, an impurity caused by touching a dead body (<term>hamrio</term> <note>original: *hamrio*; direct contact with a corpse</note>), which is considered so contagious that it spreads to other people and objects (<term>pitrid</term> <note>original: *pitrid*; indirect or secondary contact with impurity</note>). Just as all these states have their various levels, the general rule is that they can then only be purified again through <term>Ghosel</term> <note>original: *Ghosel*; a full-body ritual bath or "ghusl"</note> alone \*), for which bull’s water—

Everything defiled is purified with the <term>Nirang-i-gomez-din</term> and the <term>Zur-water</term> <note>original: *Zurwasser*; consecrated water used in Zoroastrian liturgy</note>. Hard metals and precious stones require the fewest washings. A stone is pure after six washings. Contaminated earth, however, can only become pure again after a year’s time. ## daily religious service

the temple service must be distinguished from that which the Parsi practices as religion in his natural, everyday life.

The daily temple service, which is performed by priests, is for the most part—aside from the <term>Ghosel</term> <note>original: *Ghoſel*; ritual washings or full-body ablutions</note> purifications which are frequently undertaken in the temple—contained in the reading of liturgical prayers. Each day has its Yazata, whose festival is celebrated on its day. ### Daily Religious Service

He prays to the sun three times a day: at its rising (<term>Havan watch</term> <note>original: "Gah Havan"; the period from sunrise to noon</note>), at noon (<term>Rapithwin watch</term> <note>original: "Gah Rapitan"; the period from noon to 3 p.m.</note>), and at three o'clock in the afternoon (<term>Uzayirin watch</term> <note>original: "Gah Uziren"; the period from 3 p.m. to sunset</note>) with the <term>Litany of Mithra</term> <note>original: "Neaesch Mithra's"; a prayer to the divinity of light and oaths</note>. The <term>Litany</term> <note>original: "Neaesch" or Nyayishen</note> of the moon is spoken when it becomes visible (at the new moon), on the fifth day, and when it wanes.

As often as he approaches water or fire, a <term>Nirang</term> <note>here described as a "short powerful sigh"; a brief ritual formula or incantation</note> is prayed.

Regarding nourishment and food, everything is allowed to him, except for dogs, and also nothing that <term>Ahriman</term> <note>the destructive spirit or personification of evil</note> created, such as rats, cats, snakes, wolves, frogs, etc.—all these are <term>noxious creatures</term> <note>original: "Kharfesters"; animals considered harmful to the good creation</note>.

During the meal, every <term>Parsi</term> <note>original: "Parse"</note> who makes a claim to holiness wears his <term>mouth-veil</term> <note>original: "Penom" or Padan; a cloth worn to prevent breath or saliva from contaminating sacred elements or food</note> before his face, and the meal is completed in silence. At the end of the meal, drinking is performed first, which he does with a tilt of the neck so that the drink is poured into the mouth without the lips touching the vessel. Their food is brought to the mouth with the fingers, likewise without these touching the lips. They also seek with the greatest care to prevent anything from the mouth from falling onto the clothes or the dish, for the saliva of the mouth defiles. After eating, they wash their mouths and say: "That is the will of <term>Ahura Mazda</term> <note>original: "Ormuzd"; the supreme god of Zoroastrianism</note>," etc.

->of the Parsis.<-

All their ordinary activities—cutting nails, traveling, lighting lamps, etc.—must be accompanied by short prescribed prayers. A burning light must either be extinguished by the wafting of wind <note>by waving or fanning the flame through the air</note>, or they cut it off below the flame and carry it to the fire, where it must consume itself. <note>Traditional Zoroastrian practice forbids blowing out a flame with the breath, as the breath is considered ritually impure and would defile the sacred element of fire.</note>

The Parsis do not extinguish fire or the burning of houses with water, but rather with thrown earth, stones, bricks, etc., so that it smothers and destroys itself. <note>Both fire and water are sacred; using one to "kill" the other is considered a violation of their purity.</note>

## Regarding the Deceased

### Concerning
## the Initiation into the Mazdayasnian Faith.

---

One is not a member of this faith by birth alone. The <term>Parsis</term> <note>Zoroastrians who fled to India from Persia</note> consider newborn children to be ritually unclean; touching them before the legal purification also defiles the person who touches them. This purification is performed using <term>Perahom</term> <note>original: "Perahom"; the juice of the Haoma plant (ephedra), considered a sacred drink</note>, which can be obtained from the <term>Mobeds</term> <note>Zoroastrian priests</note> and is dripped into the child’s mouth immediately after birth, before it receives its mother’s milk. Following this, the child is washed three times with bull’s urine <note>Traditionally used for its perceived spiritual and physical cleansing properties</note> and once with water. A <term>Mobed</term> or another astronomer then prepares the child’s horoscope <note>original: "Lebensprognostikon"</note>, which he provides to the parents in writing, and bestows a name (usually that of an <term>Ized</term> <note>original: "Ized"; a Yazata, a divine being or angel in Zoroastrianism</note> or a famous Persian). After three years, the father must offer a sacrifice to <term>Mithra</term> <note>the divinity of light, justice, and covenants</note> on the specific day and month that corresponds to the child's name. Until the seventh year, such a child is considered incapable of sinning; the parents merely protect it from physical impurity. After the completion of the seventh year, the child must be purified with <term>Ghosel</term> <note>ritual bathing</note> or <term>Sischoe</term> <note>a simpler form of ritual washing</note> whenever defilement occurs; at this time, the child is also eligible to wear the <term>Kosti</term> <note>the sacred girdle or thread worn by Zoroastrians</note>, for which purpose he is initi-

Anyone who neglects this is an apostate.

Foreign <term>proselytes</term> <note>converts from other religions</note> are also admitted through the <term>Bareshnum</term>, provided they have previously received instruction in the ceremonies and daily prayers, and have also made their confession of faith and vowed to follow the Law of <term>Zoroaster</term>.

Through a two-fold <term>Bareshnum</term> <note>original: "Baraschnom"; the most rigorous nine-day ritual purification</note>, and by being led for four days by three <term>Dasturs</term> <note>high priests</note> each day to the <term>Arvisgah</term> <note>the designated sacred ritual area within a temple</note>, where he reads the <term>Yasna</term> and performs a <term>Ghusl</term> <note>original: "Ghosel"; a ritual bath</note> with <term>Nirang</term> <note>consecrated bull urine used for ritual cleansing</note> and water, he becomes a <term>Herbad</term>. The other <term>Parsis</term> pay two <term>Rupees</term> (approximately 1 <term>Reichsthaler</term> 8 <term>Groschen</term> <note>historical German currency used here as a conversion for contemporary readers</note>) to a <term>Mobed</term> <note>priest</note> who performs this ceremony for them, and then they are true <term>Behdins</term> <note>literally "those of the Good Religion"; the term for Zoroastrian laypeople</note>, <term>Mazdayasnians</term>, and worshipers of Ormuzd <note>Ahura Mazda</note>. Anyone who neglects this is considered an apostate.

Through the <term>Bareshnum</term>, foreign proselytes are also admitted, provided they have previously received instruction in the ceremonies and daily prayers, and have also made the confession of faith and vowed to follow the law of Zoroaster.

<header>Initiation into the Mazdayasnian Faith.</header>

O Judges! <note>This likely addresses the spiritual authorities or the reader as a witness to the divine law.</note> The pure law of the <term>Mazdayasnians</term> <note>original: "Mazdeiesnans"; followers of Mazdayasna, the worship of the Wise Lord, Ahura Mazda</note>, the law of excellence, truth, and justice, was sent by God to the nations and was truly brought to light by the pure Zoroaster.

Through these previously described rites, the <term>Parsi</term> <note>original: "Parse"; a member of the Zoroastrian community, particularly those who settled in India</note> becomes a member of the spiritual body of the <term>Mazdayasnians</term>. Into the

### civil union

he enters through marriage, which is considered essential among them for a true <term>Mazdayasnian</term>; so much so that children are usually betrothed in their ninth year (in Surat, this happens as early as the second or third year, following Indian custom). The age of marriage is fifteen for males and thirteen for girls. A girl then has a right to demand a husband from her parents, which they may not deny her without great offense against the law; and a girl who has refused marriage until her eighteenth year must remain in hell until the Resurrection <note>original: "Auferstehung"; referring to Frashokereti, the Zoroastrian doctrine of the final restoration of the universe and the raising of the dead</note>.

The most highly regarded marital union among the <term>Parsis</term> is <term>Khetudas</term> <note>original: "Khetudas" or "Xetwodah"; a term for next-of-kin marriage, which in later tradition and as noted here, specifically refers to the practice of marrying within the family or between cousins</note>, marriage among blood relatives, and according to this explanation, between cousins.

In thoughts and deeds, may pure blessings come upon you! Speak the truth among the great; toward the <term>Behdins</term> <note>original: "Behdins"; literally "those of the Good Religion," a term Zoroastrians use to describe themselves</note>, your friends, let your countenance be cheerful and your eyes benevolent. # Marital Union

<meta>catchword: To the</meta>

is fifteen years old, his mother is wedded to her husband for a second time, and only then does she enjoy full rights as a wife. This marriage in **<term>Jog-zan</term>** <note>original: "Jog-zan"; likely referring to *Chakar-zan*, a secondary marriage status for a woman who was previously a widow</note> is not very highly esteemed.

A girl can also be purchased as a wife for a deceased youth; she is then regarded and treated as his widow. This woman must then marry another man, and the first son is legally credited to the deceased and is treated exactly as in the case mentioned above. This form of marriage is held in very high regard among the **<term>Parsis</term>** <note>The Zoroastrian community in India</note> and is called a **<term>Sader-zan</term>** <note>original: "Sader-zan"; likely *Satar-zan*, a proxy marriage arranged to provide an heir for a man who died childless</note>.

Marriages with a widow are indeed permitted but are not very highly esteemed, as her husband regards her only as his second wife. The least respected is a marriage with a girl who has rejected the man her father proposed to her and married another against his will. She can obtain full rights as a wife only if, after her first son reaches maturity (after fifteen years), she allows herself to be wedded to her husband for a second time.

The husband has many rights over his wife. In the event of her disobedience, if it lasts until the following day, he can separate himself from her. On the other hand, he is bound to be faithful to her, and adultery makes the crossing over the bridge **<term>Tschinevad</term>** <note>original: "Tschinevad"; the Chinvat Bridge or "Bridge of the Requiter," the spiritual path the soul must cross after death to reach the afterlife</note> impossible.

<meta>catchword: I.</meta>

---

**That which was created from the very beginning.** <note>original: "Das von Urbeginn an Erschaffene." This is a literal German translation of the Middle Persian title *Bundahishn*, an encyclopedic work on Zoroastrian cosmogony and mythology.</note> This is to the Parsees <note>Zoroastrians who fled to India to avoid religious persecution</note> the same as Genesis was to the Israelites. It is likely a collection of various essays or fragments dating from different periods. While it is written in the <term>Pehlvi script</term> <note>Pahlavi, the Middle Persian writing system used by the Sassanid Empire</note>, it is mixed with <term>Parsi</term> words. Some of these fragments may be of great antiquity, while others are certainly of more recent origin, as they cite later figures and events. Anyone will find the variations encountered in this book striking, which often border on contradiction; one will quite rightly view these as the different systems of their <term>Desturs</term> <note>High priests or spiritual leaders in the Zoroastrian tradition</note>. Although this book cannot be considered the first scripture of the Parsees in terms of chronology (rather, it always bases the authority of its pronouncements on the <term>Zend</term> <note>Interpretations and commentaries on the Avesta scriptures</note> and the Law), it nevertheless deserves to stand at the very beginning because of its content, as much of their doctrine refers to it and receives clarity from it.

Bundahishn. <note>original: "Bun-Dehesch." The title of the Middle Persian text meaning "Primal Creation."</note>

# I.

According to the Zend <note>The commentary and interpretation of the sacred Avestan scriptures</note>, Ormuzd and Ahriman were the only ones belonging to the host of Unlimited Time, which had shared its essence with them in the very beginning. Ormuzd <note>The Middle Persian name for Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity of goodness, light, and wisdom</note>, the glorious Ormuzd with the Law, was in time—is—and will be for all eternity. His throne and dwelling is what is called First Light, and his all-surpassing wisdom, his work, this purity, is the Law.

Ahriman <note>The Middle Persian name for Angra Mainyu, the destructive spirit and personification of evil</note>, also present through time, dwelt with his law in the darknesses. His primal dwelling was First Darkness: he—the Evil One—was alone in their midst. These two beings, swallowed up in the infinity of good and evil, without limits in their duration, lived solitary in the midst of these abysses. For the Great Ormuzd's first kingdom of light and Ahriman's primal darkness were unlimited. Nevertheless, their kingdom was limited. Ormuzd's kingdom is limited <note>This refers to the spatial boundary between the two realms, even though Ormuzd himself is infinite</note>—he himself is without any limits. Ahriman is slave—and king.

Ormuzd's people <note>original: "Volck." Here referring to the divine beings or the righteous</note> will endure endlessly and eternally in the resurrection of the dead—like the course of all existence. Ahriman's companions will vanish when the dead once more live. He himself will be without end.

From there, he unleashed the ravenous <term>Kharfesters</term> <note>original: "Kharfesters"; noxious or harmful creatures such as insects and reptiles believed to be created by the evil spirit.</note> upon the earth—those which carry poison, such as snakes, scorpions, toads, etc. From him, hot water rained down upon the trees so that they withered <margin>d)</margin>, and the cruelly tormenting <term>Berin</term> and <term>Boschasf</term> <note>Names of specific demons (Dews) representing lethargy, sickness, or physical suffering.</note> (Dews) were made to fall upon the bull and Kaiomorts to torture them at the breast. The bull died from the poison, and while dying, he spoke these words: "See what must happen for the sake of the animals that are yet to come. Gladly will I submit to my fate, if only they may be protected from the Evil One." Kaiomorts’ time had not yet come; he was destined to be king for thirty years, and after the arrival of <term>Peetiare</term> <note>The personification of adversity or the "counter-creation" of the enemy.</note>, he lived for another thirty years. Kaiomorts spoke to him: "You have come as an enemy, but all the people of my seed shall do what is pure and cast you to the ground."

### XIII.

Concerning the **Seas** <term>Zare; from the Avestan 'zrayah', meaning sea or large body of water</term> (rivers and waters), the Law teaches that the **Sea of Vourukasha** <note>In the text: "Zare’ Ferakh kand," a name meaning "wide-shored."</note> is a work of **Alborz** <note>The mythical mountain range surrounding the earth.</note> which waters the land toward the south. This sea of a thousand water-channels is like the source of the **Arduisur** <note>Aredvi Sura Anahita, the celestial river and goddess of all waters.</note>, the "palace of the streams," because it flows out from the throne of **Ormuzd** <note>Ahura Mazda, the Supreme Creator.</note>; it is superior to all other waters and is a blessing during hot days. It is purified by the Arduisur, which flows together with it in a **lake** <term>Var; a reservoir or lake</term> upon the mountain, and it possesses ten thousand golden channels.

**Syria** <note>In the text: "Sur," identified here as ancient Assyria.</note> has, among other seas, the great **Putih** <note>The Puitika Sea, which in Zoroastrian myth filters the waters of the Vourukasha.</note>. This sea appears on the side of the Vourukasha and flows together with it. In the middle of the Vourukasha Sea, the Putih forms one of its sides, which is called **Lake Satavaesa** <note>In the text: "Var Satevis."</note> after the star **Satavaesa** <note>Often identified as the star Fomalhaut or Antares, associated with the western direction and the control of tides/rain.</note> in Syria; by means of a strong wind, this star removes all decay from the water, purifying it and making it bright as light. It flows forth in great quantities and floods, pouring into the lower regions. Putih bears the name **Por-av-gar** <note>Original: "Por-av-gar," from Pahlavi 'pur-āb-kar' meaning "maker of much water."</note> (high flood or hollow water) because it swells twice in every month <margin>h) See the footnote below for the identification of these waters with the Tigris and Euphrates.</margin>.

### XIV.

Regarding the five categories of animals, the Law provides the instruction that from the marrow of the slain bull <note>The Primordial Bull, Gavyodad, who was the first animal created and subsequently killed by the spirit of destruction, Ahriman.</note>, creations of various kinds emerged, for within its marrow this seed lay hidden. From its horns grew fruits, and from its nose the species of leeks; from its blood came grapes, from which wine is prepared, and from its breast sprouted <term>Espand</term> <note>The plant *Peganum harmala*, or Wild Rue, traditionally used in Zoroastrian rituals for purification and protection against the "evil eye."</note> which serves against rot and ailments of the head.

In heaven, the seed was purified by the Bull, to which place the Moon brought it; and from this seed, <term>Ormuzd</term> <note>Ahura Mazda, the Supreme Creator.</note> first formed two bulls, one of the male and the other of the female sex. From them came all the various species of animals; therefore it is said: that <term>Ormuzd</term> created the great bull twice, initially as the First Bull and for the second time in the animals of various kinds.

From these two bulls arose three classes of animals: 1) Goats and rams, camels and bulls, then horses and donkeys for the use of the Pure <note>The "Pure" refers to the followers of Asha (Truth/Order), i.e., the righteous humans.</note>; 2) the deer and wild animals which no human hand tames; 3) <term>Avékhone'</term> <note>From the Middle Persian *ābhīgān*, referring to aquatic or water-dwelling creatures.</note> water-animals.

One became the enemy of the other; envy and hatred arrived, and one harmed the other and suffered the same in return.

Finally, the prince of the **Daevas** <note>Original: *Dews*; malevolent spirits or demons in Zoroastrianism.</note> cried out: "O humans, worship, worship the **Daevas**." **Mashyana** <note>Original: *Meschiane’*; the first woman.</note> sacrificed to the **Daeva** of envy and hatred, and now her body became deadened <note>Original: *erstorben*; implying a loss of spiritual vitality or a state of numbness.</note>. For fifty years, they did not think of any physical union. After fifty years, they begot twins, whom **Ormuzd** <note>Ahura Mazda, the Supreme Creator.</note> took from them, providing for their upbringing. Afterwards, they begot seven more pairs of descendants, both male and female. Each pair begot children until their fiftieth year, and toward the hundredth year, they died.

### XVI.

This section of the **Bundahishn** <term>Bundahishn: Meaning "Primal Creation," this is a central Zoroastrian text that explains the origins of the world and the nature of the cosmos.</term> speaks of the procreation and fertilization of living beings. Even inanimate things are divided into male and female genders. **Heaven**, **Metal**, **Wind**, and **Fire** are procreating fathers and can never be anything else; conversely, **Water**, **Earth**, **Trees**, and the **Moon** are female, without any change.

### XVII.

The law defines five types of fires:

1) **Berezesang** <note>The *Berezisavangha*, the most sublime fire that burns before the Creator and in high places.</note> before **Ormuzd** <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity.</note> and before kings.

2) **Bohfreiann** <note>The *Vohu-fryana*, the fire residing within the bodies of humans and animals that maintains life.</note> in human and animal bodies.

3) **Oruazescht** <note>The *Urva-zishta*, the fire found within the sap of plants and vegetation.</note> in the plants.

4) **Bezescht** <note>The *Vazishta*, often associated with lightning.</note> on Mount **Sapodjeguer** <note>original: "Sapodjeguer"; the author suggests this might be a volcano.</note>.

5) **Speenescht** <note>The *Spenishta*, the "most holy" fire of the domestic hearth.</note>, which serves humans for their needs (**kitchen fire**), from which the **Behram fire** <note>The *Atash Behram*, the highest grade of consecrated temple fire.</note> (in the temples) is also drawn.

All animals and birds that consume vermin, flies, ants, snakes, and locusts are listed as warriors of Ormuzd against the Kharfesters and sorcerers.

When **Kherkas** (the vulture) spots a piece of meat on the earth from a great height, he immediately swoops down and consumes it to the detriment of the **Daevas** <term>Daevas: Referred to as 'Dews' in the text; these are demonic spirits who serve Ahriman.</term>; then, as if in triumph, he rises back into the air with the flapping of his wings.

**Halka** (the cock) is an enemy to the Daevas and sorcerers. Like the dog, he keeps watch over the world.

The Law <note>Referencing the Zoroastrian religious law or the Avesta.</note> states: When the dog and the rooster fight against **Drujes** <term>Drujes: Malevolent spirits or personifications of "The Lie" in Zoroastrianism, who work against the order of Truth (Asha).</term>, they weaken them. Therefore, it is further said: Through them, all enemies of Good are defeated; their voices destroy Evil. They deserve good food. However, if one feeds them with that which is pure and prescribed, all **Daevas** <term>Daevas: Ancient demons or destructive spirits who choose to serve the cause of evil.</term> are put to shame.

->**XX.**<-

Regarding the **Rivers** <note>original: "Ruds"</note>, it is said that through the two primary rivers that originally flowed from **Alborz** <term>Alborz: Also known as Mount Hara, the mythical mountain at the center of the world from which all water and light are said to originate.</term>—the **Arang** <note>original: "Arg-rud"</note> and the **Veh** <note>original: "Veh-rud"</note>—the entire surface of the earth was supplied with water; they encircle the whole world, as they take opposing paths, and water all the **Karshvars** <term>Karshvars: The seven geographical regions or "climes" of the earth in Zoroastrian cosmology.</term>. All waters also flow back together within them. The **Avesta** <note>The primary collection of sacred Zoroastrian texts.</note> says: the heavenly Arang is **Ormuzd’s** <term>Ormuzd: The Middle Persian name for Ahura Mazda, the supreme creator god.</term> favorite; He knew him before all other rivers. Beneath him, the Veh is also pure. Ormuzd created it for twenty kingdoms. Ormuzd finds His pleasure in it; one serves the other, and both flow in harmony. Upon the approach of an enemy, they surge powerfully. A **Druj** <note>A demonic force of chaos.</note> once hindered their course, but their flow began again.

All other waters, rivers, and small springs have their origin in these and bear different names according to the places and countries they irrigate.

<meta>This page continues from the description of the world's primary rivers (the Arang and the Veh) to a detailed classification of the "fourteen waters" or fluids within the Zoroastrian cosmos, explaining how they can be defiled and how they are purified.</meta>

### **Bundahishn**

### XXI.

The Law <note>Referring to the religious codes of the Avesta.</note> names fourteen different types of water: firstly, the water on plants (the dew); secondly, that which gushes from mountains and forms **rivers** <note>original: "Ruds"</note>. The third: the rain. The fourth: **Armist** <term>Armist: Water that is found in wells or remains standing, rather than flowing freely.</term>. Fifth: the semen in human and animal bodies. The seventh <note>The source text skips the number six in this list, as the "sixth water" is revealed later as a special purification agent.</note>: the sweat on humans and animals. The eighth: the juice in the spine (marrow); ninth: what is urine in all bodies (that which passes through natural channels); tenth: the saliva. The eleventh: all oily substances in the bodies. The twelfth: the digestive juices in humans and animals; thirteenth: the tree sap that rises from below; and fourteenth: the milk of animals and humans.

If a **Nesa** <term>Nesa: A corpse or dead matter, which is considered the height of spiritual and physical pollution in Zoroastrianism.</term> (a corpse pulled from water or a drowned person) touches any of these things, then these heavenly fluids are defiled just like the rivers. Similarly, if a woman, after a premature birth and before she has been purified, even looks upon **Armist** water, the enemy of mankind <note>Ahriman, the spirit of destruction and darkness.</note> immediately becomes active. But Zoroaster has also provided for this. For **Ormuzd** <term>Ormuzd: The Middle Persian name for Ahura Mazda, the supreme Wise Lord and Creator.</term> speaks: I give you the sixth water: **Zur** <term>Zur: A sacred libation or consecrated water used in rituals to combat pollution and restore purity.</term>. Whomever you sprinkle with this reaches the first state of purity.

### XXIII.
### Origin of the Forest-Men.

Although **Jamshid** <note>The fourth legendary king of the Pishdadian dynasty, whose reign was a golden age before his fall from grace.</note>, as it is written in the Law, had a wife named **Jamag**, he nevertheless united with a sister of a **Dew** <term>Daeva: A demon or malicious spirit in Zoroastrianism.</term>, and his own biological sister **Jami** <note>original: "Djemak"</note> was forced to live with this **Dew** as if in marriage. From these unions, the forest-men with tails and sinners have their origin, as it is said: A **Dew** gave the King, in his passion, a woman from the underworld, and the King united a **Dew** with a daughter of man, beautiful as the **Paris** <term>Pairikas: Often translated as "fairies," but in this context, they are female demons or seductive spirits.</term>. They lived together, and from their mixing came subterranean beings, the godless, Negroes, and Arabs of the desert. <note>This passage reflects the historical-mythological attempt of the text's era to explain the diversity of human races and "otherness" through supernatural interference.</note> When **Fereydun** <note>The hero-king who defeated the dragon-tyrant Zahhak and restored order to Iran.</note> rose up, all these had to flee from the cities of **Iran**. After the expulsion of the **Tazians** (**Arabs**), **Fereydun** took possession of the cities of **Iran** once again.

## XXIV.

The first and most excellent among all things that are under heaven are, according to the **Avesta**:

Among humans, **Gayomard** <note>original: "Kaiomorts"; the first human in Zoroastrian mythology, created from light.</note>, whose form was white and shining with light, and whose eyes were raised toward heaven. — **Zoroaster**, the head of all and the originator of all high dignities.

Among the animals, various are named.

Among the heights, the sublime **Hukairya** <note>original: "Huguer"; a mythical mountain peak in the Alburz range.</note>, from which the shining water **Aredvi Sura** <note>original: "Arduisur"; the source of all the world's waters.</note> gushes; toward it and above it runs the star **Satavaesa** <note>original: "Satevis".</note>.

Among the plants and trees: **Haoma** <note>original: "Hom"; a sacred plant used in rituals, believed to grant immortality.</note>.

Among the rivers and waters: the red **Daitiya** <note>original: "Daeti"; a sacred river often associated with the homeland of Zoroaster.</note>.

Among the garments of men: the **Kusti** <term>Kusti: A sacred girdle or belt worn by Zoroastrians as a symbol of their faith and commitment to the religion.</term>, the crown of all clothing.

Among the <term>padyab</term> <note>original: "padiav"</note> purifications: that for which one takes the water from the **Zrayah** <note>original: "Zare’s"; referring to the great seas or lakes.</note>.

Between two men who step before **Ormuzd** <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity and creator.</note>: the one whose insight has the greatest light and whose speech has the most truth.

According to the Law, **Ormuzd** is the creator of all that exists. The world is full of the works of his hands, and everything pure that he willed, he has brought into being. Every creature of **Ormuzd** is great—visible—excellent.

### XXV.

**Ormuzd** <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity.</note> speaks thus in the Law concerning his works: I have created everything in 365 days; therefore, the six **Gahanbars** <note>original: "Gahanbars"; these are six seasonal festivals that commemorate the six stages of creation (the heavens, water, earth, plants, animals, and humanity).</note> are included within this period of time.

In the calculation of time, one names the day first and then the night, because it first became day (light) and thereafter night.

Among the months: **Farvardin**, **Ardibehescht**, and **Khordad** constitute the Spring; **Tir**, **Amerdad**, and **Schariver** constitute the heat <note>Referring to the Summer season.</note>; **Meher**, **Avan**, and **Ader** constitute the Autumn; and **Din**, **Bahman**, and **Sapandomad** are the Winter months. The sun completes its course from **Kordeh Bare’** <note>original: "Kordeh Bare’"; the zodiac sign of Aries.</note> until it returns again to this spot in 365 days and 5 small fractions of time <note>A reference to the roughly six additional hours beyond 365 days that make up a solar year.</note>; this constitutes **One Year**. In six months, it passes through six signs of the heavens, being more or less visible for 182 days, and then returns. The second year is not completely consistent with the first. To correct this, every four years a month of thirty days is extended by **One Day**, so that everything may return to its proper order.

The division of time on Earth ends with **Hamespethmedem** <note>original: "Hamespethmedem"; also known as Hamaspathmaedaya, the sixth and final Gahanbar festival, held at the end of the year to honor the souls of the dead.</note>, which falls on the last day of the last month, **Sapandomad**; and at the end of **Sapandomad** occurs the **Equinox** <note>original: "Nacht- und Tagesgleiche"; specifically the Vernal Equinox, marking the start of the Persian New Year (Nowruz).</note>.
