Each of these regents up to **Fereydun**, who is the tenth in descending line from him, is given a hundred years, thus a total of a thousand years, and this is called the reign of **Jamshid** in Persia. **Fereydun’s** lineage is a new dynasty in Persia of five hundred years. Just as in Arabia **Zohak’s** <note>original: "Zohaks"; Zahhak or Aži Dahāka, often depicted as a demonic dragon-king</note> descendants constitute a dynasty under the name: **Zohak’s** reign of a thousand years among ten members. Between **Hoshang** and **Jamshid**, this genealogy also lists a **Tahmuras** <note>original: "Tehmurets"; the "Demon-Binder," a king of the Pishdadian era</note>, whose reign is stated in the chronologies as 30 years, a son of **Pedjehan** whose father is called **Hoschend**. Perhaps this is the aforementioned **Hoshang**, or a collateral line of his.

# **Bundahishn**
<note>original: "Bun-Dehesch"; The Bundahishn, or "Primal Creation," is a foundational Zoroastrian text detailing the creation of the world, its history, and the eventual triumph of good over evil.</note>

->L<-

All of time is completed in twelve thousand years.
It is written in the Law: that the heavenly people <note>The spiritual creations of Ahura Mazda, existing in a state of pure spirit</note> were alone during the first three thousand years; at that time, the army of the Enemy <note>The evil spirit Ahriman and his demons</note> did not venture out into the world, and they were not yet known. **Gayomard** <note>original: "Kaiomorts"; the mythological first human</note> and the **Primal Bull** <note>The first animal, from whose essence all later life sprang</note> comprise another three thousand years. These millennia of God are reflected in the first six celestial signs: **Aries** <note>original: "Lamm" (Lamb)</note>, **Taurus** <note>original: "Stier" (Bull)</note>, **Gemini** <note>original: "Zwillinge" (Twins)</note>, **Cancer** <note>original: "Krebs" (Crab)</note>, **Leo** <note>original: "Löwe" (Lion)</note>, and **Virgo** <note>original: "Kornähre" (Ear of Corn)</note>. These encompass the aforementioned six thousand years.

After the millennia of God came **Libra** <note>original: "die Wage" (the Balance)</note>: the **Adversary** <note>original: "Peetiare"; referring to the onset of the "Great Assault" by the spirit of evil, Ahriman, which polluted the perfect creation</note> rushed out into the world.

**Gayomard** lived for thirty years alongside the enemy of nature.

After thirty years, **Mashya** and **Mashyana** <note>original: "Meſchia und Meſchiane"; the first human couple who, according to legend, grew out of the earth in the form of a rhubarb plant</note> appeared on the earth, and after fifty years they felt the desire for procreation. Their lifespan was ninety-three years.

**Tahmuras** <note>original: "Tehmurets"; a legendary king of the Pishdadian dynasty known for subduing demons</note> reigned for thirty years.

**Jamshid’s** <note>original: "Djemſchids"; one of the most famous kings of Persian myth, credited with establishing civilization</note> reign and glory were completed in 613 years and 6 months. After this, he continued for another 100 years, but in hiding and unknown.

After the millennia of God comes **Scorpio** <note>original: "the Scorpion"</note>, and **Zahhak** <note>original: "Zohak"; the tyrant king with serpents growing from his shoulders who usurped the throne</note> was powerful for a thousand years.

After the millennia of God comes **Sagittarius** <note>original: "the Bogen-ſchütz" (Archer)</note>: **Fereydun** <note>original: "Feridun"; the hero-king who overthrew Zahhak and restored the rightful lineage</note> reigned for five hundred years.

The <term>Vendidad</term> <note>The name means "The Law Against the Demons"</note> is the only surviving part (<term>Nosk</term> <note>one of the twenty-one traditional books or divisions of the Zoroastrian scriptures</note>) of what is known in the true and specific sense as the <term>Avesta</term>, or the legal instruction that <term>Zoroaster</term> <note>the prophet Zarathustra, active in ancient Persia</note> received from the mouth of <term>Ormuzd</term> <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity of Zoroastrianism</note> and delivered to humanity. Its name already indicates its content: *Revelations against the <term>Dews</term>* <note>Daevas; malevolent spirits or demons in Persian mythology</note>. It contains legal prescriptions against all forms of impurity, for every impurity is viewed as a hiding place in which the Dews conceal themselves to gain access to people. This Vendidad now serves as the primary religious work for the <term>Parsis</term> <note>Zoroastrians who fled to India to escape religious persecution</note>, since they have been forever deprived of the other Nosks of their Avesta.

Where have all the other books of this Avesta gone? Even the Parsis cannot give a satisfactory account of this. Today's <term>Desturs</term> <note>high priests within the Zoroastrian faith</note> blame Alexander the Great, who, during the conquest of Persia, is said to have set these books aside shortly after their creation, burning six of them and taking the remaining fourteen with him, thus robbing them of this precious treasure for all time. Whether this legend is grounded

It also describes the Parsi tradition that Alexander the Great destroyed or stole the other twenty volumes of their sacred scriptures.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the lost books of the Avesta, specifically addressing the historical credibility of the claim that Alexander the Great was solely responsible for their destruction. # Vendidad.

if this claim were grounded, it would contradict the reports found in the surviving catalogs regarding the contents of those lost books. While these lists do acknowledge the loss of several volumes of the *Avesta*—which *Alexander* may have committed to the flames out of religious zeal—they suggest that many others were merely mutilated by him. In those cases, he supposedly removed certain sections but left the remainder behind. Thus, other persecutions must have affected these books, or perhaps these damaged fragments were simply not treated with the same care and holy devotion as the fully preserved *Vendidad*. Such negligence may have eventually led to their complete loss.

Perhaps the subsequent wars between the *Seleucids* <note>the Hellenistic dynasty that ruled Persia after Alexander's death</note> and the local rulers of *Iran*—whom the Seleucids viewed as *usurpers* <note>original: "Usurpateurs"</note>—also proved fatal to this religion and its sacred texts. Ultimately, the blame for all of this was laid at the feet of *Alexander*, whom the people regarded as the original author of their misfortune.

The *Parsis* also speak of a great upheaval caused by *Mani* <note>the prophet Mani, founder of Manichaeism, who sought to "complete" Zoroastrianism</note> during the reign of *Ardeschir* <note>Ardashir I, the 3rd-century founder of the Sassanid Empire</note> (in the third century of the Christian era). This sect was further supported by his successor *Schapur* (*Sapores* <note>the Latinized version of the name Shapur</note>) and grew rapidly in number. However, despite the success of this sect against the *Magi* <note>the traditional Zoroastrian priestly class</note>, the instability of those times likely made it impossible to locate these books of the *Avesta*, even if they were still held in the few temples where they were kept for ritual use,

<summary>This page analyzes historical theories regarding the loss of the Avesta, suggesting that while Alexander the Great is traditionally blamed, the loss was likely a result of centuries of war, religious competition from Manichaeism, and a lack of preservation for damaged texts.</summary>

# Vendidad.

...[it was possible] to completely destroy them, as their existence must have been too well-known to report their plunder more reliably and to avoid the predicament in which the lack of all records concerning this event now places them.

This *Vendidad* <note>a collection of texts within the larger *Avesta* primarily concerned with religious law and ritual purity</note> is now the most essential part of religion for the *Parsis* <note>the Zoroastrian community in India</note>, as well as for their worship in the temples, where it must be read (daily?) according to its divisions. It is always accompanied by the prescribed prayers from the *Izeschne* <note>the *Yasna*, the primary liturgical collection of the Zoroastrians</note> and *Visperad* <note>a set of supplements to the *Yasna*</note>: and this recitation possesses such power that the *Dews* <note>demons or malevolent spirits in Zoroastrianism</note> tremble before it, and the *Izeds* <note>the *Yazatas*, or divine beings worthy of worship</note> draw near to protect the *Mazdayasnians* <note>literally "worshippers of Mazda," the formal name for followers of the religion</note>.

*Vendidad* is *Pa-zend* <note>referring to *Pazend*, a system of writing that uses the Avestan alphabet for Middle Persian</note>—that is, the meaningful foreign expressions and words incorporated into the *Zend* <note>the sacred language and its interpretation</note> must not be translated or expressed in another language, for they would then lose all their power and efficacy. It must therefore be read in the ancient language. It has been translated into *Pahlavi* <note>Middle Persian</note>, with the exception of the 12th *Fargard* <note>chapter</note>. In India, a translation of the first six *Fargards* into the *Sanskrit* language is also said to exist.

The sections and divisions in the *Vendidad* bear the name: *Fargard*. In their language, this word signifies a "separation" or a "tearing away." It is probable that this book was originally written as a continuous sequence without any divisions,

But the death-pregnant **Peetiare’ Ahriman** <note>original: *Peetiare’*; from the Avestan word for "adversary" or "opposition," referring to the counter-creations of the evil spirit</note> created there, and in all the villages, the harsh winter, the work of the **Dews** <note>Daevas, or malevolent spirits and demons</note>.

These places and cities were pure and crossed with fruit-bearing valleys: these lands were without any filth or defilement.

Abundance and **Behescht** <note>Paradise; the Persian term for the highest heaven or state of bliss</note> are for the righteous man who is pure. The holy one is pure, he who performs heavenly and pure works.

## II. Fargard <note>Chapter</note>.

Zoroaster asked **Ormuzd** <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme creator deity of Zoroastrianism</note>: O Ormuzd, enveloped in glory, righteous judge of the world which exists through your power, you who are purity itself: which man first questioned you, as I am doing? You, who are Ormuzd, to whom did you reveal the law of the god of Zoroaster? Ormuzd spoke: The pure **Djemschid** <note>Jamshid (Yima), a legendary king of the golden age in Iranian mythology</note>, head of the peoples and the herds, was, O holy Zoroaster, the first man who sought me, Ormuzd, as you do now. To him, I opened the law of the god of Zoroaster.

I, who am Ormuzd, encouraged him: devote yourself to my law, pure Djemschid, son of **Vivengham** <note>Vivanghat</note>, contemplate it, and bring it to your people. Alas! answered the pure Djemschid, I am not righteous enough to perform your law, to contemplate it, and to bring it to mankind. Thereupon

### III. Fargard.

Righteous Judge of the world, who bears your power, you self-eternal Purity! what is the first thing that pleases this earth, and makes it favorable to us?

Righteous Judge, etc. what is the second thing that pleases this earth? h)

It pleases the Earth, and she becomes favorable to us, when a righteous and powerful man prepares healthy, elevated places for priests and herds, women and children, pure places of assembly; then all will thrive in purity. Likewise, when one levels the earth and plants it with grain, trees, etc.; when one promotes its fertility; and also cares for the animals of the house and field, so that they may mate.

## Vendidad.

Whoever levels the land and sows seeds for grain, herbs, and fruit trees within it, irrigates it and makes it fertile, to him the land will say: Your cities shall multiply in number and abundance! May your land bear fruit and grain in wealth and plenty. But where this does not occur, the earth will speak: Pure and healthy foods shall remain far from your place. May <term>Darudj Nesosch</term> <note>original: "Darudj Nesosch"; referring to Druj Nasu, the Zoroastrian demon of corruption and pollution</note> plague you! The purest point of the law of the <term>Mazdeiesnans</term> <note>original: "Mazdeiesnans"; followers of Mazda-worship or Zoroastrianism</note> is: to sow strong seeds into the earth with purity. Whoever does this is regarded as though he had given life to a hundred creatures, or produced a thousand things, or recited ten thousand <term>Izeschnes</term> <note>original: "Izeschnes"; the Yasna, or primary liturgical acts and prayers of the Zoroastrian faith</note>. # Vendidad.

The transgressions of <term>Mithra-Darudj</term> <note>original: "Mithra-Darudj"; literally "the lie to Mithra," referring to the breaking of a contract or promise, as Mithra is the divinity presiding over covenants</note> 1) are of six kinds: 1) He who gives his word and does not keep it, 2) he who places his hand in the hand of another without loyalty in his heart, doing so with injustice and a deceitful intent, 3) he who promises a reward to a tame animal and unjustly robs it of the same, 4), 5), 6) he who does the same to a wild animal, or its master (gamekeeper), or toward entire villages and every field laborer.

These sins are punished proportionally with three hundred to a thousand years' duration in hell. Yet this can be averted by an equal number of <term>Riemenstreiche</term> <note>lashes or strokes with a leather strap</note> which he must suffer as penance here, or with an offering of the same number of <term>Derems</term> <note>original: "Derems"; an ancient currency</note> which, if the punishment is not paid by the man himself, his heirs must still pay for him. If someone dies as a <term>Tanafur</term> <note>original: "Tanafur"; a state of mortal sin where the soul is considered forfeit and unable to cross into paradise</note>, these things must be done for him: speak a pure word on his behalf, and send pure and holy wishes to heaven for him. ### Abundance and Paradise, etc. <note>The original German uses "Behescht," the Persian word for Paradise.</note>

# Fifth Fargard. <note>A "Fargard" is a chapter or section of the Vendidad, the part of the Avesta focused on ritual purity and ecclesiastical law.</note>

If a person dies in a field (on fertile land) or on the street, it could easily happen that a bird of prey might soon fall upon this corpse and thereby defile a tree upon which it perches with its beak, so that this wood would become unusable for fire because it is impure. <term>Ormuzd</term> <note>original: "Ormuzd"; the Middle Persian name for Ahura Mazda, the supreme creator god of Zoroastrianism</note> commanded great caution in this matter to the pure <term>Mazdeiesnans</term> <note>original: "Mazdeiesnans"; literally "Mazda-worshippers," the name for followers of the Zoroastrian faith</note> as soon as they see that such a bird has perched upon a tree. To avoid this danger, it was ordained that this corpse be quickly moved away from the vicinity of such things, so that neither bird, nor dog, nor wolf, nor the wind might defile anything with the dead; otherwise, it would make the person a criminal.

The water is not defiled if a person drowns in it and the fish immediately consume him. Neither is the fire defiled if someone burns and dies within it.

The one who has died on the street or through a misfortune shall be brought to such a <term>Zad-marg</term> <note>original: "Zad-marg"; likely referring to a "place of death" or a site designated for the handling of a corpse before its final disposition</note> (a place

## VIII. Fargard. <note>A "Fargard" is a chapter or section of the Vendidad, the book of the Avesta focused on ritual purity and law.</note>

In the winter time, when rain and snow make the path to the <term>Dakhmé</term> <note>The "Tower of Silence" or place where the deceased were exposed to nature</note> inaccessible, a <term>Mazdeiesnan</term> <note>A Mazdayasnian, or a worshiper of the supreme god Ahura Mazda (a Zoroastrian)</note> must not leave his dead lying there. These five acts are guilty of <term>Tanafur</term> <note>A category of serious sin (Avestan: *Tanapuhr*), literally meaning "body-forfeit." These were sins originally considered so grave that they required severe physical penance or were seen as putting the soul's salvation at great risk.</note>:

It is not permitted to strike a pregnant dog, to abandon her, or to steal her young. Whoever does so shall suffer seven hundred lashes of the strap.

## XVII. Fargard.

<note>A Fargard is a chapter or section of the Vendidad, a book of the Avesta focusing on ecclesiastical laws and rituals.</note>

Whoever cuts or pulls out their hair while grooming it, or clips their nails without following the legal prescriptions, thereby releases the <term>Dews</term> <note>Also known as Daevas; in Zoroastrianism, these are malevolent spirits or demons that cause spiritual and physical corruption.</note> upon the earth, as well as the <term>Khrafstars</term> <note>Harmful creatures like insects, snakes, or predators believed to be the creation of the evil spirit Ahriman.</note>, which people call lice, and which live in plants and clothes; he thereby increases death as much as any worshiper of the Dews.

If he has done this through carelessness or oversight, he must remove this waste to a distance of ten <term>Gams</term> <note>A *gam* is a ritual pace or step used as a measurement of distance.</note> from pure people, twenty from fire, thirty from water, and fifty from the bound <term>Barsom</term> <note>A sacred bundle of twigs or metal rods used by priests during Zoroastrian ceremonies.</note>. He places the hair on a stone while reciting the victorious words: "Let, O holy <term>Ormuzd</term> <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme creator deity.</note>, all trees grow in abundance," and draws three, six, or nine <term>Keischs</term> <note>Ritual furrows or circles drawn in the sand or earth to create a spiritual boundary or containment zone.</note> around the stone, during which he must recite the <term>Honover</term> <note>The *Ahuna Vairya*, one of the most sacred and ancient Zoroastrian prayers.</note> (that is: "Ormuzd's Will," etc.) each time. The nails he places on a stone facing the direction that is Ormuzd’s property <note>margin: This likely refers to the land of Iran, just as within Iran it refers to the region of Mount Alborz.</note>, and speaks the victorious words: "O holy <term>Bahman</term> <note>Vohu Manah, or 'Good Mind,' one of the Amesha Spentas (Holy Immortals) who represents divine wisdom.</note>, I pray to you with purity." Draw the circles around the same stone again, and speak the Honover at each one. Then he says: "Bird <term>Aschozescht</term> <note>The Ashozushta bird, often identified as an owl, which in Zoroastrian myth devours the "nails" (demons) to prevent them from becoming weapons for the Dews.</note> <note>margin: This bird is sacred to Bahman.</note> I direct my prayer to you, I call upon you..."

### Abundance and Paradise, etc.
## XIX. Fargard.

From the north and all northern regions rushes <term>Ahriman</term> <note>Angra Mainyu; the primordial spirit of evil and destruction in Zoroastrianism.</note>, the first of the <term>Dews</term> <note>Daevas; a class of malevolent spirits or demons who serve Ahriman.</note>, pregnant with death. This <term>Darudj</term> <note>The Druj; the personification of "the Lie," deceit, and cosmic disorder.</note> roams the world, murdering and tormenting, and teaching the evil law.

I spoke the <term>Honover</term> <note>The Ahuna Vairya; the most sacred and ancient prayer in Zoroastrianism, believed to have the power to repel evil.</note>, O <term>Zoroaster</term> <note>Zarathustra; the founding prophet of the faith.</note>, and performed the <term>Izeschné</term> <note>The Yasna; the primary liturgical ceremony involving the ritual sacrifice and purification of water.</note> to the pure water; I set the pure law in motion, and so this Darudj, murderer and teacher of the evil law, withdrew in a faint. This Darudj, the over-proud Ahriman, wanted to defy me to my face—he had not yet seen the holy Zoroaster surrounded by radiance and glory. This hell-demon saw Zoroaster with but a single glance and recoiled. He saw that Zoroaster would tread him underfoot and stride along like a victor—he saw that <term>Akuman</term> <note>Aka Manah; the demon of "evil mind" or "bad thoughts," who is the direct opponent of Good Mind (Vohu Manah).</note>, murderer and source of all evils, would be utterly destroyed. He, with his long and widely extended arm, roamed the earth, and cared nothing for <term>Ormuzd</term> <note>Ahura Mazda; the supreme creator god of light, wisdom, and goodness.</note>, the Great, the Judge of Righteousness—and after a long journey, he moved into—<term>Poroschasps</term> <note>Pourushaspa; the earthly father of Zoroaster.</note> house. Zoroaster is more powerful than Ahriman.

Envy, evil, fever, weakness and their originators, greed, unnatural lusts, deafness and blindness of the spirit, the serpent, lies, hideous malice, destruction, and the impure poison that <term>Ahriman</term> <note>The supreme spirit of darkness and destruction.</note> has brought to the human body; all impure desires shall flee, as shall death and all types of magic, whose teachers are the <term>Paris</term> <note>original: "Paris"; the Pairikas, seductive female spirits or witches who use sorcery to corrupt the world.</note>. All <term>Darvands</term> <note>original: "Darvands"; the followers of the "Lie" (Drug), representing the unrighteous or wicked people.</note> will be destroyed.

In this law-wishing Ariema, O Zoroaster, people will once again enjoy pure joys, so that <term>Bahman</term> <note>Vohu Manah, or "Good Mind," one of the Amesha Spentas (Holy Immortals) who represents divine wisdom and protects animals.</note> rewards the purity of their hearts and their thirst for the law. Let them be even purer, even more fervently zealous for the law, and they shall be the beloved of the great Ormuzd. This law-desiring Ariema will conquer all impure desires, all kinds of death, and the magic that the Paris teach. It will conquer all Darvands.

This is Ormuzd's will: that the head of the law perform pure and holy works. Bahman blesses with abundance the one who acts holily in the world.

<summary>This concluding section of the 22nd Fargard describes a ritual of purification involving ninefold offerings and symbolic furrows to banish the 99,999 diseases and demonic influences of Ahriman. It promises a restoration of joy and divine favor for those who remain zealous in following the Zoroastrian law.</summary>

I cannot explain the expression **Vendidad Sade** more clearly than as: the accompaniment of the **Vendidad**. The Parsees’ **Vendidad Sade** encompasses the three books: the **Vendidad**, **Vispered**, and **Izeschne'** <note>Also known as the Yasna, the primary liturgical collection of Zoroastrianism</note>. It belongs entirely to the temple service and must be read aloud in the <term>Avestan language</term> <note>original: Zendsprache; the ancient Eastern Iranian language in which the scripture was composed</note>, although translations in <term>Pahlavi</term> <note>A Middle Persian language and script used for religious commentaries</note> and, for some parts, in the local vernacular also exist. The **Vendidad** must never be read alone; it must always be accompanied by the **Vispered** and the **Izeschne'**. 

The **Vispered** consists almost entirely of invitations to prayer and hymns of praise, even when it occasionally breaks out into these praises itself. Therefore, it is understandable when it is said that the **Vispered** cannot be read alone, or without the **Izeschne'**. The hymns of praise in the **Vispered** and the prayers of the **Izeschne'** often flow into one another so much that they seem almost identical; even within the collection, various prayers from the **Vispered** and **Izeschne'** are so intermingled that they could be considered as one. Furthermore, based on their content, it appears that several of these prayers are read before the recitation of the **Vendidad**, while others are read after it. However, these details of their liturgy <note>original: Gottesdienst</note> do not interest us quite as much.

# Visperad <note>original: Wispered; a collection of supplements to the Yasna, the primary Zoroastrian liturgy, used during seasonal festivals</note>

# Yasna <note>original: Izeschnë</note>
<header>Izeschné.</header>
<sig>R 3</sig>

I call upon and exalt the pure water, all waters created by **Ormuzd** <term>Ahura Mazda; the Supreme Creator</term>; all trees created by Ormuzd.

I exalt and call upon the pure and excellent word completed by **Zoroaster**, the **Vendidad** <term>Vendidad; the "Law Against the Demons," a book of the Avesta focused on purity and ritual law</term> given to Zoroaster, this sublime, pure, and long-lasting law of the worshipers of Ormuzd.

I call upon and exalt highly the Mountain of Life <note>Likely referring to Mount Hara Berezaiti</note>, Ormuzd’s creature, in its brilliant light; and all radiant mountains, the seat of bliss, created by Ormuzd; the light of the **Kayanids** <note>original: Keans; the legendary dynasty of Persian kings</note> created by Ormuzd <gloss>r)</gloss>; the light of the **Ervads** <note>original: Herbeds; a rank of the Zoroastrian priesthood</note> created by Ormuzd.

I call upon and exalt highly **Ashi** <note>original: Aschesching; the divinity of fortune, reward, and spiritual wisdom</note>, the pure wisdom, pure greatness, pure justice, and the beneficent light created by Ormuzd.

I call upon and exalt highly **Dahman** <note>original: Dahman; likely Dahman Afrin, the spirit of the community's blessing</note> the Pure, who brings joy to the people and to righteous men, the strong seed of the heavenly people.

I call upon and exalt places and cities, the places of the herds, houses of blessing and abundance; water; earth; trees; the pure earth, the pure wind, the moon, the star of beneficence; the sun, the divinely created primal light; all people of the being enveloped in glory, the holy, pure, and great people.

# Yasna <note>original: Izeschné</note>
<header>Izeschne.</header>

I call upon and exalt highly the pure and great **Bordj** <term>Mount Alburz/Hara Berezaiti; the cosmic mountain in Zoroastrian cosmology from which the sun rises</term> <gloss>s)</gloss> of the times, days, **Gahs** <term>the five traditional periods of the Zoroastrian day</term>, moons, **Gahanbars** <term>the six seasonal festivals</term> and years—and the holy and great **Vendidad** <note>The book of ritual laws</note> given to **Zoroaster**.

I call upon and exalt highly the pure **Fravashis** <note>original: Feruers; guardian spirits or pre-existent souls</note>, strong and well-armed: the Fravashis of the **Paoiryo-tkaesha** <term>original: Poeriodeskeschans; "the people of the first law," referring to the righteous ancestors and ancient saints</term>, the Fravashis of my own people <note>the adherents of the Zoroastrian Law</note>, and the Fravashi of my own soul.

I call upon and exalt highly all holy leaders <note>original: Häupter; heads or chiefs</note>.

I call upon and exalt highly all pure-born **Yazatas** <note>original: Izeds; divine beings worthy of worship</note> in heaven and in this world; I bring them praise, and a pure, paradise-worthy **Nyayesh** <term>original: Neaesch; a humble prayer of petition or praise</term>.

If a man offends you <note>Addressing Ormuzd/Ahura Mazda</note> through his thoughts, his words, or his deeds, whether driven by passion or not, and he humbles himself before you and calls upon you, then be a friend to him, O **Ormuzd** <term>Ahura Mazda; the Supreme Creator</term>, holy, pure, and great, more excellent and greater than all: just as I also am a friend again to the man who offends me through thought, word, or deed, whether driven by passion or not, if he humbly asks it of me.

t) These words: "I bring Khshnuman," and: "I exalt the purity," etc., are repeated alternately with each indicated object, such as: "I bring Khshnuman to the Haoma; I exalt the purity of the **Barsom**" <term>a bundle of sacred twigs or metal rods used in the ritual</term>, etc. To "bring Khshnuman" means among the **Parsis** <note>the Zoroastrian community</note>: to cite something distinctive about this person or thing, or a quality of theirs that is beneficial to mankind. The omitted **Has** <note>chapters</note> are entirely similar to these, as they contain almost the same objects, only with variations in expression; sometimes it says: "I worship"; then: "With this **Zaothra** <term>original: Zur; a consecrated water libation</term>, with this Barsom, I worship"; then: "I bring Khshnuman, I bring the Yasna <note>original: Izeschne</note>, I bring the **Nyayesh** <note>original: Neaesch; prayer of praise</note> to this," etc.

The first grace for which I ask you is that I may attain the glorious dwellings of the saints, which shine entirely in light and bliss. The second grace: that my body may eternally remain in good condition. The third is length of life. The fourth grace is to be always great, happy, and powerful, to destroy evil and annihilate the *Darudj* <term>Darudj; the Druj, or the personification of the Lie, deceit, and chaos</term>. The fifth grace for which I ask you, O death-destroying *Hom*, is that you may always watch over me—

<note>original: Jeſchts Sades; the 'Yashts' are a collection of twenty-one hymns of praise dedicated to specific Zoroastrian divinities or 'Yazatas' (beings "worthy of worship"). <meta>This page continues the introduction to the Yashts, following the half-title page of Book Two. It explains the liturgical function and structure of these hymns within the Parsi tradition.</meta>

# The Yashts

The **Yashts** consist also of praises and prayers, which I cannot better bring under a general category than by the term: **Festival Prayers**. Every month and day, as well as every division of the day (<term>Gah<note>The Zoroastrian day is divided into five 'Gahs' or watches, each with its own prayers.</note></term>), has a specific <term>Yazad<note>original: Jzed; a divinity or angelic being 'worthy of worship' in the Zoroastrian faith.</note></term> under whose supervision they stand, and whose name they bear: it is to these that the Yashts are addressed, which are also read on their designated days. They are composed in <note>original: Zend; refers here to the Avestan language</note>, yet are also translated into the common vernacular. The <term>Parsis<note>The Zoroastrian community in India, descended from Persian refugees.</note></term> possess only eighteen of these Yashts, as the others have been lost. The accompaniment to these Yashts, which gives them the name **Yasht Sadeh** <note>The term 'Sadeh' (pure/plain) refers to manuscripts containing only the sacred text without the Pahlavi commentary.</note>, consists mainly of the <term>Nyayishes<note>original: Neaeschs; litanies or 'humble, obedient prayers' addressed to specific deities like the Sun or Moon.</note></term>, which share almost identical subjects with them and are incorporated into these Yashts nearly word-for-word; however, there are also some pieces from the **Yasnas** <note>original: Jzeschne's; the primary liturgical service and its associated texts.</note> that are inserted here and there as short prayers. In various festivals, the places of the lost Yashts are filled by <term>Has<note>original: Ha's; the chapters or subdivisions of the Yasna liturgy.</note></term> from the Yasna, which thereby also become festival prayers, in order [to compensate for] the loss of the Yashts

<summary>This page defines the Yashts as festival prayers dedicated to specific divinities (Yazads) and explains the "Yasht Sadeh" format, which combines these hymns with litanies and sections from the Yasna.</summary>
<keywords>Yashts, Yazads, Gah, Yasht Sadeh, Nyayishes, Yasna, Parsi liturgy, Avestan language, liturgical structure</keywords>

--- Page 362 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 299 regarding how specific chapters (Has) from the Yasna liturgy are used to fill the gaps left by the lost Yasht hymns.</meta>

# Yashts.
<meta>catchword: These</meta>

to replace. Some of these <term>Has<note>Chapters or subdivisions of the primary Zoroastrian liturgical text, the Yasna.</note></term> indicate in their headings the very day on which they serve as <term>Yashts<note>Hymns of praise addressed to specific divinities.</note></term>; thus the 28th Ha has the title: **Gahan-Yasht** <note>original: Gahan-Jescht; this refers to the section containing the Gathas, the most ancient and sacred hymns composed by the prophet himself.</note>, which includes all following chapters up to the 52nd Ha, and this Yasht is read on all those days in which the <term>Gahs<note>The five watches or "shifts" of the Zoroastrian day.</note></term> and <term>Gahanbars<note>Six seasonal festivals that commemorate the stages of the world's creation.</note></term> (festivals in memory of the creation) are celebrated. Even the specific calendar days of the <term>Haftenghat<note>The Yasna Haptanghaiti, or the "Yasna of Seven Chapters," an archaic Avestan text.</note></term>, <term>Ushtavaiti<note>original: Oschtuet; one of the five Gathas or poetic hymns of Zoroaster.</note></term>, etc., for which specific Has are intended, are noted. Thirteen Has (namely from 54 to 66) are called, as festival prayers: **Srosh-Yasht** <note>original: Serosch-Jescht; hymns dedicated to Sraosha, the divinity of conscience and divine obedience.</note>, and the last six bear the title: **Setut-Yasht** <note>original: Setut-Jescht; likely the Stot Yasht, a portion of the liturgy dedicated to songs of praise.</note>.

This is proof that from the most ancient times, the followers and successors of Zoroaster have considered it forbidden to substitute their own works for the works of their great teacher, or to replace the lost pieces from their own reflections; instead, they preferred to designate other prayers for this use, which they knew had one and the same author as the lost pieces. In general, for anyone who becomes familiar with these writings, the suspicion is increasingly confirmed—and rises almost to certainty—that no one but Zoroaster composed these essays and gave them their entire structure. One should examine, for example, the content and expression of the 31st and 32nd Ha; they are entirely appropriate to Zoroaster’s personal situation, but in the mouth of anyone else, they would lose their internal truth.

<summary>This page argues that the Zoroastrian community preserved the integrity of their sacred texts by using existing chapters by Zoroaster to replace lost hymns, rather than inventing new ones. The author cites specific chapters of the Yasna (Has 31 and 32) as evidence of Zoroaster's unique and authentic authorship.</summary>

# Yashts.

This collection of prayers, which Anquetil <note>Abraham-Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron (1731–1805), the French scholar who famously brought the first Avestan manuscripts from India to Europe.</note> brought back from the Orient under the name **Yasht Sadeh** <note>original: "Jescht Sade"; the term "Sadeh" (meaning 'pure' or 'plain') refers to manuscripts that contain only the Avestan text without accompanying ritual instructions or Pahlavi translations.</note>, contains, in addition to these public liturgical prayers, others that are partly daily prayers of the **Parsis** <note>original: "Parsen"; the Zoroastrian community in India.</note> and partly intended for specific occasions. Some are characteristic and serve to provide a complete insight into this religion; for this reason, I shall not withhold them from my readers, even if they only serve to help one become acquainted with the mindset of a people who drew everything—even the most insignificant actions of life—into their religion.

<summary>The author introduces the 'Yasht Sadeh' collection of prayers brought to Europe by Anquetil-Duperron, noting that they reflect the Zoroastrian tendency to integrate religious practice into every aspect of daily life.</summary>
<keywords>Anquetil-Duperron, Yasht Sadeh, Parsis, Zoroastrianism, daily prayers, liturgical texts</keywords>

# Yasht = Ormuzd <note>d</note>

May my prayer please **Ormuzd** <note>The Middle Persian name for Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity and creator in Zoroastrianism, representing light and wisdom.</note>! May he crush **Ahriman** <note>The personification of evil and darkness, the eternal antagonist of Ormuzd.</note>, and fulfill my wishes until the Resurrection.

Abundance and **Paradise** <note>original: "Behescht"; referring to the "Best Existence" or heaven for the righteous.</note> are for the righteous who is pure; he is holy who is pure, and who performs heavenly and pure works.

->In the name of God!<-

Ormuzd, King of Glory, may your fame and your splendor increase ever more, O Ormuzd, Judge of Righteousness.

Ormuzd, light and shining with glory, Heavenly One of the Heavenly, come to my protection!

I repent of all my sins and renounce them.

O Ormuzd, be gracious to me; I offer you the **Yasna** <note>original: "Izeschne"; the primary liturgical service and collection of texts in the Avesta.</note> and **Niyayish** <note>original: "Neaesch"; specific prayers of praise and petition recited at particular times.</note>.

is entirely identical to the <term>Nyaish</term> <note>original: "Neaesch". These are shorter Zoroastrian litanies of praise.</note> of the Moon. # Nyaishs

are known among the <term>Parsees</term> <note>Zoroastrians living in India who preserved these ancient texts.</note> as humble and obedient prayers. Specifically, they designate a certain class of prayers established for the praise of the <term>Izeds</term> <note>original: "Izeds" or Yazatas—divinities or "venerable beings" who act as protective spirits under Ormuzd.</note>. In their content, they are identical to the Yashts; only their different usage determines the distinction between them. Yashts are strictly consecrated for temple service, whereas through the Nyaish, every Parsee can and should turn to the Ized to offer his requests and praise. For this purpose, they have also been translated into the common vernacular of the country.

One can view these Nyaishs as an excerpt from the Yashts. The Yashts list in detail, as it were, all the attributes of the Ized—their excellence and beneficence, which the

According to the author's intent, they are meant to be a means for the Parsee to frequently occupy himself with this benefactor, and to exalt the one from whom he enjoys all good things.

->In the name of God!<-

You who have been merciful since the very beginning, generous, rich in goodness, powerful, wise, pure. Nourisher and Sustainer of all that exists. Righteous King, your sovereignty is without change. Ormuzd, King of Glory, let the greatness and radiance of the Sun increase—the sun which does not die, which streams radiance all around and runs like a victorious hero.

->In the name of God!<-

I repent for all my sins and renounce them, etc. <note>original: "2c." An abbreviation for "etcetera."</note>

(three times)

### Patet.

...against <term>Khordad</term> <note>Haurvatat, the Archangel or Amesha Spenta presiding over water and wholeness.</note> and the water sources, against <term>Amerdad</term> <note>Ameretat, the Archangel or Amesha Spenta presiding over plants and immortality.</note> and the various species of trees, etc. <note>The text uses "2c." as an abbreviation for "etc." (et cetera).</note> *) for all these sins I beg forgiveness, etc.

<term>Sader</term> and <term>Khetudas</term> <margin>q)</margin> are necessary. If I have now neglected these and the various prayers commanded of me, I beg forgiveness for this sin, etc.

If I have promised <term>Patet</term> <note>A prayer of confession or repentance.</note> for someone else and neglected it, or [if I have neglected it] regarding the evil actions of another, or have not named each error specifically: for these sins I beg forgiveness, etc.

# Patet.

...I, who belong to Ormuzd <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme god of wisdom and light.</note> and am of his pure people.

I choose the right and pure path, and I forsake all paths of error. I strike and shatter Ahriman <note>Angra Mainyu, the spirit of evil and destruction.</note>, and offer <term>Setaesch</term> <note>Setayesh; praise or worship.</note> to Ormuzd, the Glorious and Great.

## Patet Mokhtat (of the Soul).

This is the previous Patet, which the <term>Mobed</term> <note>A Zoroastrian priest.</note> recites for the deceased in the third person (where previously the person spoke in the first person) and adds at the end:

The sins that [Name] <note>Original: "N. N.", a placeholder for the name of the deceased.</note> has committed, or could have committed from the beginning, I lament in his stead; I, who through the fact that he commanded it of me, am united with him, just as the giver of alms becomes one with the one who receives the alms. For him, I bear sorrow for the sin that he committed through thought, word, and deed. Forgive them for him; they cause me pain: I repent of them through the three words <note>The Zoroastrian ethical triad: Good Thoughts, Good Words, and Good Deeds.</note>, and bear sorrow for his failings.

---

...[to have] performed, for which he pays him. This no one may neglect who does not wish to be an apostate from the Law.

# Afergans and Afrins.

---

Blessings and songs of praise that belong to the temple service on certain festivals, especially the <term>Gahanbars</term> <note>Festivals held six times a year to commemorate the stages of the creation of the world.</note>. Their content consists of well-wishes for the people and for the king — also for the deceased, and they are celebrated annually on the anniversary of their death.

<note>original: "Afrinam Kschetrian," a prayer for the sovereignty or the blessing of the ruler.</note>

May the <term>House of Song</term> <note>The highest heaven or "Garothman," literally the "Abode of Song"; original: "Gorotman."</note> be its reward, its prize! Oh, may all noble deeds of noble souls, including those who have already died, and my own noble deeds, reach these holy souls!

Whatever is commanded for the sins of a soul, whether committed out of weakness or through calculated vice; whatever must be performed for the redemption of the soul when it has taken its leave from this world—be it the <term>Myazda</term> <note>A ritual meal offering; original: "Miezd."</note> or the <term>Yasna</term> <note>The primary liturgical service or sacrifice; original: "Izeschne."</note>: whoever has performed these, let them also be remembered by me here. May their sins vanish, and their noble works increase! May the soul hear this <term>Patet</term> <note>A prayer of repentance or confession; original: "Patet."</note> and accept it! This is what my soul wishes for all the living creations of <term>Ahura Mazda</term> <note>The supreme creator deity; original: "Ormuzds."</note>.

Be merciful to me, <term>Ahura Mazda</term> <note>original: "Ormuzd."</note>, Judge of Justice, you who shine in light and glory!

# Afergan <note>The Afringan or "Blessing" is a Zoroastrian ceremony of praise and benediction; original: "Afergan."</note>

My mouth speaks this <term>Afrin</term> <note>A prayer of blessing or benediction.</note>. # Nerengs

<note>Nerengs are short liturgical formulas or incantations believed to possess spiritual power; original: "Nerengs."</note> are daily prayers of the <term>Parsis</term> <note>The Zoroastrian community in India; original: "Parsen."</note> arranged for all occurrences of human life. *Nereng* means *power*, and through the use of these prayers, which are often spoken only as <term>Badj</term> <note>A ritual silence or a prayer recited in a low, suppressed whisper; original: "Badj."</note> (as silent sighs, softly), their explanation is that every deed and undertaking of theirs will succeed better.

## Prayer upon Falling Asleep and upon Waking.

->In the name of God!<-

Help me, <term>Ormuzd</term> <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity and creator in Zoroastrianism, representing light and wisdom; original: "Ormuzd."</note>, King of Glory; watch over me. May <term>Peetiare'</term> <note>The spirit of opposition, harm, or the "adversary"; original: "Peetiare'."</note> not harm me. <term>Mithra</term> <note>The divinity of light, contracts, and friendship; original: "Mithra."</note> and <term>Serosch</term> <note>Sraosha, the divinity of hearing and obedience, who protects the soul at night; original: "Serosch."</note> help me and care for me. O <term>Ormuzd</term>, let the names: <term>Ormuzd</term>, <term>Amschaspand</term> <note>The Amesha Spentas, the "Holy Immortals" or divine emanations of God; original: "Amschaspand."</note>, <term>Mithra</term>, <term>Serosch</term>, <term>Raschne-rast</term> <note>Rashnu the Just, the divinity who judges the souls of the deceased; original: "Raschne-rast."</note>; let all these names be highly praised!

### Upon Waking.

Abundance and <term>Behescht</term> <note>Paradise or the "Best Existence"; original: "Behescht."</note> etc. I pray with purity of thought, purity of word, and purity of deed. O God, great and glorious Judge! I repent for all my sins: I believe firmly in God and His law and the heavenly nature of my soul. At the resurrection, the abyss shall be filled, and <term>Ahriman's Dews</term> <note>The demons or malevolent spirits serving Ahriman, the spirit of darkness; original: "Ahrimans Dews."</note> shall be reduced to nothing.

The blessed of <term>Behescht</term> sing: I sing the <term>Gah Oschtuet</term> <note>Refers to the Gatha Ushtavaiti, hymns of enlightenment and "happiness" from the Yasna; original: "Gah Oschtuet."</note> <note>u)</note> with purity. O <term>Ormuzd</term>, let every pure person, whoever they may be, attain the fulfillment of their and my wishes.

The damned of <term>Duzakh</term> <note>The place of punishment or "the difficult existence," equivalent to hell; original: "Duzakh."</note> say: Which place shall we call upon? Which prayer shall we choose?

## Nereng for Washing the Hands.
->(Prayer during the washing of the hands.)<-

In the name of God!

Ormuzd, King of Glory, grant that <term>Serosch</term> <note>Sraosha, the divinity of hearing, obedience, and protection who guards the world at night; original: "Serosch."</note> may grow in glory and radiance—the Pure and Strong, whose fame is vast and great, the King in Ormuzd's world; send him for my protection.

# Nereng <note>Short ritual prayers or protective incantations; original: "Nereng."</note>

<margin>x) Through this, he simultaneously performs his prayer to this <term>Gah</term> <note>A specific period or "watch" of the day in the Zoroastrian calendar; original: "Gah."</note>. Daily, the <term>Parsis</term> <note>Followers of the Zoroastrian faith in India; original: "Parsen."</note> must call upon each Gah at the appointed hour.</margin>

I exalt <term>Ushahin</term> <note>The "Oschen" or the watch from midnight until the first appearance of the stars; original: "Oschen."</note> x) the holy, pure, and great; I long for his love and vow to him: Ushahin, who gives sublimity to all places.

May pure <term>Sraosha</term> <note>The divinity of "Obedience" and "Hearing," a protector of the soul; original: "Serosch."</note> be favorable to me; I highly praise him, the holy, pure, and great victorious hero Sraosha, who blesses the world with abundance.

The <term>Honover</term> <note>The Ahuna Vairya, one of the most sacred and ancient Zoroastrian mantras; original: "Honover."</note> protects my body.

O <term>Ormuzd</term> <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme God of light and wisdom; original: "Ormuzd."</note> my God, watch over me, so that I may take vengeance upon the <term>Devas</term> <note>Demonic spirits or false gods; original: "Dews."</note> who wish me ill. Protect me, my God, through fire and <term>Vohuman</term> <note>The archangel "Bahman," representing Good Purpose and protector of animals; original: "Bahman."</note>, so that I may have the strength to do good.

I direct my prayer to the sweet earth.

I exalt Sraosha and bless him with strength. Grow forever in the radiance of light and bliss. Enjoy in happiness health by the thousands and ten thousands.

I worship the great, living, most pure Ormuzd; the created <term>Verethragna</term> <note>The divinity of Victory; original: "Behram."</note>, the constant guardian who penetrates all things; <term>Ram-Kvastra</term> <note>The divinity of peace and the atmosphere; original: "Rameschne - Kharom."</note>, the bird who acts from on high and protects the world; and I worship you, who like a bird watches over the world, a being enfolded in glory; you, the celestial revolution, created by God out of <term>infinite time</term> <note>The concept of Zurvan Akarana, or time without bounds; original: "unbegränzten Zeit."</note>.

# Nereng <note>Short ritual prayers or protective incantations; original: "Nereng."</note>

# Explanation
## of the foreign names and words that occur in the Parsee scriptures.

---

### A.

**Ader**, the name of the ninth month, also of a guardian angel (<term>Ized</term> <note>A class of Zoroastrian divinity or benevolent spirit; original: "Izeds"</note>), who manifests in the radiance of fire; also the holy fire itself. Usually
**Aderan** is the holy fire in the <term>Dadgah</term> <note>The "place of the law," referring to a consecrated area for a sacred fire; original: "Dadgah."</note>.
**Adoscht**, the stone upon which the fire-vessel stands in the temple.
**Afergans** and **Afrins**, prayers of praise and wishes for blessings.
**Afrasiab**, King in Turan, an enemy of <term>Ke Khosro</term> <note>A legendary king of the Kayanian dynasty in Persian mythology; original: "Ke Khosro's."</note>.
**Aguerefte** is the intent to strike another <note>Refers to a specific category of sin or legal offense in Zoroastrian tradition involving the threat of physical violence.</note>.
**Akuman**, the first evil spirit created by <term>Ahriman</term> <note>The personification of evil and the "Destructive Spirit" in Zoroastrianism; original: "Ahriman."</note>.
**Albordi** is likely the Caucasus mountain range, which is described as the foundation, root, and bedrock of the entire earth.

## of the foreign names and words.

**Amerdad**, the seventh among the <term>Amshaspands</term> <note>The Amesha Spenta, or "Bounteous Immortals," who are divine beings created by the supreme god; original: "Amſchaſpands"</note>, also the name of the fifth month.

**Amrosh**, the bird that distributes the fruit-seeds present in <term>Ferakh kand</term> <note>Likely referring to the Vourukasha, the primordial sea in Persian cosmology where the Tree of All Seeds grows; original: "Ferakh kand"</note> across the earth.

**Amshaspands** are the first and most exalted spirits surrounding <term>Ormuzd’s</term> <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme creator and god of light; original: "Ormuzds"</note> throne.

**Anahid**, an <term>Ized</term> <note>A Yazata, a divinity or benevolent spirit worthy of worship; original: "Ized"</note> who preserves the seed of Zoroaster, from which, in the end times, <term>Oschederbami, Oschedermah, and Sosiosch</term> <note>The three promised saviors in Zoroastrian prophecy who appear at intervals of a thousand years; original: "Oſchederbami, Oſchedermah und Soſioſch"</note> are to be conceived.

**Ander**, a <term>Dew</term> <note>A Daeva, an evil spirit or demon in service to the darkness; original: "Dew"</note>, created by <term>Ahriman</term> <note>The spirit of destruction and evil; original: "Ahriman"</note>.

**Apevesh Apotschereh**, a <term>Dew</term> who seeks to obstruct river and rain water.

**Ard**, an <term>Ized</term> (<term>guardian spirit</term> <note>original: "Schutzgeiſt"</note>).

**Aredosch**, the sin committed when one strikes another out of hatred.

**Arjesp**, King in Turan, adversary of Zoroaster and his law.

**Ardibehescht**, an <term>Amshaspand</term>, also the name of the second month.

**Arduisur**, a spring that flowed from Ormuzd’s throne during creation; she is called Ormuzd’s daughter and is an <term>Ized</term>.

**Arez**, the fish that constantly sits upon the head of Ahriman’s toad <note>In Zoroastrian myth, the Kar fish (Arez) guards the sacred White Haoma tree from a toad created by Ahriman to destroy it.</note>.

**Arg-rud** and **Veh-rud**, two rivers that Ormuzd allows to flow around the entire earth to distribute their water.

**Ariema** is the land, or rather the capital of the land of Iran, which first accepted the law and is dearly loved by Ormuzd.

# of Foreign Names and Words.
Aa

**Bordj** signifies the "navel" on the mountains from which the water gushes forth. Specifically, it also refers to the peak of the **Alborz** <note>original: "Albordj"; the high mountain range in Northern Iran</note>, from which the sun and moon emerge in their courses; in this sense, it is called:
->**Bordj of the Ages**, from which the ages, as it were,<-
->gush forth.<-

**Boschasp**, a <term>Daeva</term> <note>original: "Dew"; an evil spirit or demon in Zoroastrianism</note> who induces sleep and who mortally wounded the Primordial Bull.

**Burzin**, also **Burzin-matun** or **Burzin-meher**, a fire worshipped by **Vishtaspa** <note>original: "Gustasp"; the king who first patronized Zoroaster</note>; it is said to represent lightning and is also called the "Fire of the Laborers" <note>This refers to the *Adur Burzen-Mihr*, one of the three Great Fires of ancient Iran</note>.

---

## D.

**Dad-gah** (Place of Justice) is the name of a smaller Parsi temple; it is also sometimes called the **Jadamarg**, where the dead are brought before they are taken to the **Dakhme**.

**Daeti**, see **Tschekaet Daeti** <note>A reference to the mythical mountain *Chakad-i-Daitik*, the center of the world</note>.

**Dahman**, a <term>Yazata</term> <note>original: "Ized"; a benevolent divinity</note> and **Hamkar** (assistant or companion) of the watch of **Behestveschtrosch**; he receives the souls of the righteous from the hands of **Sraosha** <note>original: "Serosch"; the divinity of conscience and obedience</note> and leads them to heaven.

**Dakhme**, the burial place of the Parsis <note>often called a "Tower of Silence"</note>; it must be situated at a distance from everything pure, on an elevated, dry location, and must be fenced in. According to the law, it should be destroyed every 50 years.

**Damavand** <note>original: "Darnavand"</note>, a mountain to which **Zahhak** <note>original: "Zohakh"; the demonic dragon-king</note> was chained by **Fereydun** <note>original: "Feridun"</note>.

**Drujes** <note>original: "Darudjs"</note> are the creatures of **Ahriman** <note>the spirit of darkness and evil</note> that devastate the world.

# Explanation

**Darun**, small sacrificial breads offered in honor of Dahman and Haoma <note>original: "Homs"; the sacred plant and divinity of the Zoroastrian liturgy</note> during various festivals and occasions.

**Darvand**, a name for Ahriman <note>the spirit of darkness and evil</note>, which is also applied to evil people.

**Daschtan**, refers to when a woman has her "sickness" <note>menstruation</note>, during which time she keeps herself sequestered.

**Deratht**, plants or growths.

**Derem**, a small coin; also used as a unit of weight.

**Derimher**, (Gate of Mercy) <note>original: "Thür der Barmherzigkeit"; refers to the *Dar-e Mehr*, a term for a Zoroastrian fire temple</note> is the name of the great Parsi temple in Surat <note>original: "Suratte"; a major center for the Parsi community in India</note>.

**Destur**, the first class among the priests and their scholars. **Destur Mobed** is the one who supervises the others. **Desturan Destur** is the highest rank, formerly the <term>Chief Magus</term> <note>original Latin: "Archimagus"; the supreme leader of the Magi</note>.

**Dew**, is an epithet for Ahriman after he became evil, and all his creatures are called **Dews** <note>demons or evil spirits</note>; they exist in both male and female sexes, the latter of which are called **Paris** <note>original: "Paris"; likely referring to *Peris*, though in earlier mythology these were often seen as mischievous or fallen spirits</note>.

**Dewiesnan**, "Worshippers of the Dews"; a term for all those who do not accept the law of Zoroaster.

**Djamasp**, one of the foremost figures at the court of King Vishtaspa <note>original: "Ke Gustasp"</note> and a friend of Zoroaster.

**Dje**, a **Dew** of impurity who seduces people into a dissolute life.

**Djemschid**, an ancient king <note>the mythical King Jamshid</note> who accepted the teachings of Haoma <note>original: "Hom"</note> regarding the one highest God; he is said to have been cast into the abyss because of a single sin, but was also redeemed from it.

**Din**, the name of the tenth month; also a <term>Yazata</term> <note>original: "Ized"; a benevolent divinity</note>.

**Freschosfer**, a brother of **Djamasp** <note>Jamasp, a wise vizier and early follower of Zoroaster</note>, who assisted **Zoroaster**.

### G.

**Gahanbars** are joyous festivals commemorating the creation, established by **Djemschid** <note>Jamshid, the mythological fourth king of the Pishdadian dynasty</note> and distributed throughout the entire year; they are also worshipped as **Izeds** <note>Yazatas; divine beings or "angels" worthy of worship</note>.

**Gahs** <term>Gah: one of the five specific periods into which the Zoroastrian day is divided</term> is the name for the divisions of the day, which are under the protection of specific **Izeds**. During the **Farvardians** <note>The festival of the souls of the deceased, mentioned on the previous page</note>, their festivals are also celebrated in a special manner.

**Gathas** is the name of the festivals where the **Gahs** and **Gahanbars** are celebrated. <note>While the Gathas are primarily known today as the seventeen hymns composed by Zoroaster, this text identifies them as festival periods in the liturgical calendar</note>

**Gam**, a measure of 3 feet <note>original: "Maaß von 3 Fuß"</note>.

**Ghosel**, a type of purification <note>Ghusl; ritual washing or ablution</note> among the **Parsis**.

**Gogard** is the name of **Hom** <note>Haoma, the sacred plant and divinity of healing</note>, and also of a tree in **Ferakh kand** <note>The mythical Vourukasha Sea, previously identified as the Indian Ocean</note>.

**Gorotman** <note>Garothman, literally the "House of Song"</note> is the place of joy and light where the souls of the righteous are led after death.

**Goschasp**, also **Ader-Goschasp** <note>Adur Gushnasp, one of the three great sacred fires of ancient Iran, associated with the warrior class</note>, a sacred fire that **Ke Khosro** <note>Kay Khosrow, a legendary king of the Kayanian dynasty</note> established on Mount **Asnevand**.

**Goschorun** <note>Geush Urvan; the "Soul of the Kine"</note>, the soul of the first-created bull, was elevated to an **Izeds** and brings about fertilization.

**Guerschasp** <note>Garshasp</note>, an ancient hero of **Iran**.

**Gueti-Kerid** <gloss>buying the heavenly world; original: "die himmlische Welt kaufen"</gloss> refers to when a fifteen-year-old **Parsi** has a paid **Mobed** <term>Mobed: a high-ranking Zoroastrian priest</term> perform the holy service for eight days in his own name. If he neglects this, he is considered an apostate, and should he die in this state, he cannot enter **Behescht** <note>Paradise</note>.

**Hesar**, a measure of approximately 3000 steps. <note>likely a version of the Persian "Hazar" (thousand), referring here to a specific distance</note>

**Hom**, in antiquity, was the founder of the worship of the One God and has been elevated to an **Ized** <note>Yazata; a divine being worthy of worship</note>: the Hom-tree <note>Haoma; a sacred plant in Zoroastrian ritual</note> is sacred to him, and its juice is praised as a special means for revitalization and purity.

**Honuet**, one of the **Gatha** festivals. <note>The Gathas are the five intercalary days at the end of the year, each associated with a hymn of Zoroaster</note>

**Honover**, is the living and powerful word of **Ormuzd** <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity</note>: "I will!" Among humans, **Honover** is performed when they confess: "That is **Ormuzd’s** will," which is believed to possess special power. <term>Honover: Refers to the Ahuna Vairya, the most sacred Zoroastrian prayer</term>

**Huraschmodad**, is 1) the beginning of the day. 2) the heavenly rooster, who, like **Serosch** <note>Sraosha; the angel of obedience and protection</note>, protects mankind and frightens away the **Dews** <note>Daevas; demons or malevolent spirits</note> with his voice at daybreak.

**Huguer** or **Tireh Albordj**, the topmost peak of **Albordj**. <note>Mount Hara Berezaiti, the mythological mountain at the center of the world</note>

### J.

**Jog zan**, is a second marriage that is permitted to the **Parsis** alongside the first (**Schah zan**). <term>Jog zan (Chakar Zan): A secondary marriage status, often for widows; Schah zan (Shah Zan): A woman’s first marriage, carrying full legal status</term>

**Ized**, signifies a guardian spirit or guardian angel of the visible world, and all high spirits—even **Ormuzd** himself—are considered **Izeds** from this perspective. <note>From the Avestan 'Yazata', meaning 'one worthy of worship'</note>

**Izesch-Khane**, is the secluded, sacred place within the **Derimher** <note>Darb-e Mehr; literally "Gate of Mithra," the common term for a Fire Temple</note> in **Surat**, where the **Vendidad**, **Izeschne** <note>The Yasna; the primary liturgical act of worship</note>, etc., are read and their divine service is celebrated.

### K.

**Kaiomorts** was the first human, who arose from the right hip of the slaughtered bull, from whose—

**Nam-zad**, the betrothal among the Parsis. <note>original: "die Verlobung bey den Parsen"</note>

**Nekah**, the marriage blessing.

**Nereng**, (Force and Strength) is 1) a means of purification consisting of ox urine (it is called **Nereng Gomez Din** once it has been consecrated), 2) a type of prayer that the Parsi recites daily. <note>Nereng or Nirang: In ritual use, consecrated bull urine (Nirang-din) is used for spiritual and physical cleansing in Zoroastrianism</note>

**Nesoschs** are entire swarms of <term>Dews</term> who fall upon the corpse to steal it. <note>Dews: Daevas, or demonic spirits; the "Nasu" demon specifically takes the form of a fly to infect the dead</note>

**Nimruz**, means midday, when **Rapitan** rules. <note>Rapithwin: the spirit of the midday heat and the summer season</note>

**No-zud**, is the ceremony through which a Parsi earns the name **Herbed** <note>Ervad: the first rank of the priesthood</note>; at the age of 15, accompanied by three <term>Desturs</term> <note>Dasturs: high priests</note>, he performs the service of the <term>Izeschne</term> <note>Yasna: the main liturgical service of Zoroastrianism</note> in the temple for four days. Those who cannot or will not do this may perform the **Gueti-Kherid**. <note>Geti-kharid: a ritual performed to gain spiritual merit or "purchase" a place in heaven</note>

**Oscheder bami**, Zoroaster’s son, who is still expected and will bring one-third of the earth to accept the Law. <note>The first of three promised saviors born from Zoroaster's lineage</note>

**Oscheder mah**, the second son of Zoroaster, who is to come to lead the second third of humanity to the Law.

## P.

**Peteschem**, the third <term>Gahanbar</term>. <note>Paitishahya: the third seasonal festival, celebrating the harvest</note>

**Poeriodekeschans** or **Peischdadians** were people of the first law, which **Djemschid** introduced. <note>Paoiryo-tkaesha: those of the "first faith"; Pishdadians: the first legendary dynasty of Persian kings, of which Jamshid (Djemschid) was the most famous</note>

**Poroschasp**, Zoroaster’s father. <note>Pourushaspa: the historical or mythological father of the prophet Zarathustra</note>

**Putih**, the Tigris River.

## R.

**Rameshne Kharom**, <term>Ized</term> <note>Ized: or Yazata, a divine being "worthy of worship" in Zoroastrianism, similar to an angel or lesser deity</note> of happiness, bestows prosperity.

**Rapitan**, <term>Ized</term> and second <term>Gah</term> <note>Gah: one of the five specific periods or "watches" into which the day is divided</note> of the day from noon until the afternoon. Worshipped only during the summer. <note>original: "Rapitan"; commonly known as Rapithwin, the spirit of the midday heat and the summer season</note>

**Rashne-rast**, <term>Ized</term>. <note>original: "Rašné-rast"; Rashnu the Just, the divinity who presides over the judgment of the soul after death</note>

**Raspi**, a priest for as long as he assists the <term>Djuti</term> <note>Djuti: or Zoti, the lead officiating priest in a ritual</note> in holy service.

**Ravaets**, the name for the explanations and interpretations of the <term>Avesta</term> <note>Avesta: the primary collection of Zoroastrian sacred scriptures</note> provided by their scholars. <note>original: "Ravaets"; referring to the Rivayats, a collection of traditional responses to religious questions</note>

**Ruds**, are rivers.

**Ruzgar**, the name for the day on which the anniversary of a person's death is celebrated every year.

## S.

**Sader**, **Sader (Sater) zan**, a form of marriage where a woman bears children for a deceased youth, acting as his widow even while wedded to another man; these children then carry the name of the deceased. <note>original: "Sader zan"; this refers to a proxy marriage system (Stur) designed to ensure that a man who died childless still has heirs to perform his memorial rites</note>

**Sag-did**, (the dog sees) a necessary ceremony performed with corpses, where a dog gazes upon the body so that the <term>Deivs</term> <note>Deivs: Daevas, or malevolent spirits/demons</note> are driven away from it. <note>Sag-did: the "dog-sight" ritual. In Zoroastrian tradition, the gaze of a "four-eyed" dog (one with spots above the eyes) is believed to repel the demon of decay</note>

**Sapandomad** or **Espendarmad**, an <term>Umshaspand</term> <note>Umshaspand: Amesha Spenta, one of the seven "Bountiful Immortals" or archangels who represent aspects of God</note> and the name of the twelfth month. <note>Spenta Armaiti, the divinity associated with holy devotion and the earth</note>

**Sare’ Avand**, the lid of the *Avand* or water vessel.

**Sareseok**, the bull *Hazeiosh*. <note>original: "Sareseok"; referring to the mythological ox Srisok or Hadhayans, which was said to help humans cross the ocean in ancient times</note>
